NCK MCQ Compilation (Set 3) — Answers & Rationales Compiled from newly supplied NCK exam / revision sets (FQE Paper 1 & 2, AMREF PP3 & PP4, NCK practice sets). Each question shows all four choices with the correct answer in RED, followed by a rationale referenced to approved Kenyan nursing materials (NCK curriculum & examination criteria, Kenya MOH / KEPH, Kenya IMNCI, Basic Paediatric Protocols, Kenya Essential Medicines / BNF, Brunner & Suddarth, Myles Textbook for Midwives). MCQs only. Questions accurate for both cadres are listed under each. Answer letter always agrees with the rationale. BScN BScN — Paper I Source: FQE Paper 1 — KRCHN Diploma (June 2024) 1. In barium swallow studies: A. Patients should not be NPO B. High fiber diet is encouraged a day to study C. Good for studying condition of ascending colon D. Good for diagnosing achalasia Answer: D. Good for diagnosing achalasia Rationale: Barium swallow (esophagography) visualises the esophagus and is the classic study for achalasia, showing the dilated esophagus with distal 'bird-beak' narrowing (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). Patients are kept NPO before the study, so 'not NPO' is wrong, and it studies the upper GI tract, not the ascending colon. 2. Esophageal varices are caused by: A. Inflammation of the esophagus B. Peptic ulcers C. Hepatic hypertension D. Hemorrhoids Answer: C. Hepatic hypertension Rationale: Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins resulting from portal (hepatic) hypertension, most often due to cirrhosis (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). The option 'hepatic hypertension' best represents portal hypertension; inflammation, peptic ulcers and hemorrhoids do not cause esophageal varices. 3. The following is the correct order of abdominal assessment: A. Inspection, percussion, auscultation, palpation. B. Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation. C. Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation. D. Inspection, auscultation, palpation, percussion. Answer: B. Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation. Rationale: Abdominal assessment follows inspection, auscultation, percussion, then palpation; auscultation precedes percussion/palpation so bowel sounds are not altered by manipulation (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing). 4. The following gastrointestinal disorder is managed best by downscaling gluten containing meals: A. Irritable bowel syndrome B. Diverticulum C. Celiac disease D. Esophageal varices. Answer: C. Celiac disease Rationale: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten and is managed by a lifelong gluten-free diet (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). IBS, diverticulum and esophageal varices are not gluten-driven. 5. Nursing intervention should be a priority in one of the following patients: A. Patient with appendicitis with pain rating of 10/10. B. Patient with appendicitis with sudden relief of pain. C. Patient with peptic ulcers who need omeprazole D. Patient with jaundice that need evaluation of liver function Answer: B. Patient with appendicitis with sudden relief of pain. Rationale: Sudden relief of pain in appendicitis suggests perforation/rupture, a surgical emergency requiring priority intervention (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). Severe steady pain, routine omeprazole, and elective liver-function evaluation are lower priority than a possible rupture. 6. The scientific study of the aging process is referred to as: A. Ageism B. Geriatrics C. Gerontic D. Gerontology Answer: D. Gerontology Rationale: Gerontology is the scientific study of the aging process and older adults; geriatrics is the clinical/medical care of the elderly, and ageism is prejudice against them (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg, gerontologic nursing). 7. Drug dosages must be reduced in the elderly because: A. Cardiac output is significantly reduced B. The mucosal cells in the gastrointestinal tract are reduced C. Drug biotransformation takes longer in an older person D. There is a high likelihood of manifestation of toxic effects of drugs Answer: D. There is a high likelihood of manifestation of toxic effects of drugs Rationale: Age-related decline in hepatic metabolism and renal clearance leads to drug accumulation and a high likelihood of toxicity, so doses are reduced (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg; Kenya EML pharmacology principles). This is the overarching reason encompassing slower biotransformation. 8. Nursing measures to deal with sensory changes in the aged include A. Increasing lighting in the room B. Speaking in low tones C. Providing single and adequate calories D. Suggesting appetite stimulants before meals Answer: A. Increasing lighting in the room Rationale: Aging causes visual decline; increasing (glare-free) lighting compensates for sensory changes and improves safety (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg, gerontologic nursing). Speaking in low tones worsens presbycusis; the other options address nutrition, not sensory changes. 9. Bone changes associated with aging frequently result from loss of: A. Calcium B. Magnesium C. Vitamin A D. Vitamin C Answer: A. Calcium Rationale: Age-related bone changes (osteoporosis/osteopenia) result from loss of bone calcium and mass (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). Magnesium and vitamins A/C are not the primary lost element in aging bone. 10. All of the following statements concerning genitourinary system changes in the older adult are true except: A. The glomerular filtration rate decreases B. Acid-base balance is restored more slowly C. Bladder capacity increases with advanced age D. Urinary frequency, urgency, and incontinence are common. Answer: C. Bladder capacity increases with advanced age Rationale: This is the 'except' (false) statement: with aging, bladder capacity DECREASES, contributing to frequency, urgency and incontinence, while GFR falls and acid-base correction is slower (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 11. One of the following is true about loss of muscle mass in the elderly: A. It also known as osteopenia B. It is solely caused by disused C. Exercise has no impact on the process D. It is referred to as sarcopenia. Answer: D. It is referred to as sarcopenia. Rationale: Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength is termed sarcopenia; osteopenia refers to low bone mass, and exercise/resistance training does slow the process (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 12. An example of exocrine glands are the: A. Adrenals. B. Ovaries. C. Parathyroids. D. Sweat glands. Answer: D. Sweat glands. Rationale: Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface; sweat glands are exocrine. Adrenals, ovaries and parathyroids are endocrine (ductless, secrete hormones into blood) (Anatomy & Physiology / Brunner & Suddarth). 13. The nurse knows that the anterior pituitary gland is responsible for secreting all of the following except the: A. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). B. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH). C. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). D. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Answer: B. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Rationale: This is the 'except': ADH (and oxytocin) are secreted by the posterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary secretes ACTH, FSH and TSH (Anatomy & Physiology / Brunner & Suddarth). 14. The major structure balancing the rapid action of the nervous system with slower hormonal action is the: A. Hypothalamus. B. Pineal gland. C. Hypophysis. D. Thyroid gland. Answer: A. Hypothalamus. Rationale: The hypothalamus links the rapid nervous system with the slower endocrine system by controlling the pituitary, balancing neural and hormonal regulation (Anatomy & Physiology / Brunner & Suddarth). 15. Diabetes insipidus is a disorder related to a deficiency of: A. Growth hormone. B. Prolactin. C. Oxytocin. D. Vasopressin. Answer: D. Vasopressin. Rationale: Diabetes insipidus results from deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), causing polyuria and polydipsia (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 16. When thyroid hormone is administered for prolonged hypothyroidism, the nurse knows to monitor the patient for: A. Angina. B. Depression. C. Mental confusion. D. Hypoglycemia. Answer: A. Angina. Rationale: Thyroid hormone replacement increases myocardial oxygen demand; in prolonged hypothyroidism, especially with underlying CAD, it can precipitate angina, so the nurse monitors for it (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 17. The preferred medication for treating hypothyroidism is: A. Lithium. B. Proprandol. C. Propylthiouracil. D. Synthroid. Answer: D. Synthroid. Rationale: Synthroid (levothyroxine/T4) is the drug of choice for hypothyroidism replacement (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg; Kenya EML). Propylthiouracil and propranolol treat hyperthyroidism, and lithium is unrelated. 18. A clinical manifestation not usually associated with hyperthyroidism is: A. A pulse rate slower than 90 bpm. B. An elevated systolic blood pressure. C. Muscular fatigability. D. Weight loss. Answer: A. A pulse rate slower than 90 bpm. Rationale: Hyperthyroidism produces tachycardia, elevated systolic BP, weight loss and fatigability; a pulse slower than 90 bpm is NOT associated (it would suggest hypothyroidism) (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 19. Patients with hyperthyroidism are characteristically: A. Apathetic and anorexic. B. Calm. C. Emotionally stable. D. Sensitive to heat. Answer: D. Sensitive to heat. Rationale: Hyperthyroid patients have increased metabolism causing heat intolerance, nervousness and irritability; they are not calm, apathetic or emotionally stable (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 20. Iodine or iodide compounds are used for hyperthyroidism because they do all of the following except: A. Decrease the basal metabolic rate. B. Increase the vascularity of the gland. C. Lessen the release of thyroid hormones. D. Reduce the size of the gland. Answer: B. Increase the vascularity of the gland. Rationale: This is the 'except': iodine/iodide compounds DECREASE the size and vascularity of the thyroid gland and reduce hormone release and BMR, which is why they are given preoperatively (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 21. The objectives of pharmacotherapy for hyperthyroidism include: A. Destroying overreactive thyroid cells. B. Preventing thyroid hormonal synthesis. C. Increasing the amount of thyroid tissue. D. All of the above. Answer: B. Preventing thyroid hormonal synthesis. Rationale: The objective of antithyroid pharmacotherapy (e.g., propylthiouracil, methimazole) is to inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). Destroying cells is radioiodine (not pharmacotherapy proper), and increasing thyroid tissue is opposite to the goal, so 'all of the above' is wrong. 22. Signs of thyroid storm include all of the following except: A. Bradycardia. B. Delirium or somnolence. C. Dyspnea and chest pain. D. Hyperpyrexia. Answer: A. Bradycardia. Rationale: This is the 'except': thyroid storm causes tachycardia, hyperpyrexia, delirium/somnolence and cardiorespiratory distress; bradycardia is not a feature (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 23. Medical management for thyroid crisis includes: A. Intravenous dextrose fluids. B. Hypothermia measures. C. Oxygen therapy. D. All of the above. Answer: D. All of the above. Rationale: Management of thyroid crisis includes IV dextrose/fluids for hypermetabolic demand, hypothermia (cooling) measures for hyperpyrexia, and oxygen therapy for increased metabolic demand (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 24. Pharmacotherapy for thyroid storm would not include the administration of: A. Acetaminophen. B. Iodine. C. Propylthiouracil. D. Synthetic levothyroxine. Answer: D. Synthetic levothyroxine. Rationale: Thyroid storm is treated with PTU, iodine and acetaminophen (for fever); administering synthetic levothyroxine (more thyroid hormone) would worsen the crisis and is therefore not included (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 25. The most common type of goiter is etiologically related to a deficiency of: A. Thyrotropin. B. Iodine. C. Thyroxine. D. Calcitonin. Answer: B. Iodine. Rationale: Simple (endemic) goiter, the most common type, is caused by iodine deficiency (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg; addressed in Kenya via salt iodization). This is the basis of nutritional iodine supplementation. 26. The nurse knows that the most common and least aggressive type of cancer is: A. Anaplastic. B. Follicular adenocarcinoma. C. Medullary. D. Papillary adenocarcinoma. Answer: D. Papillary adenocarcinoma. Rationale: Papillary adenocarcinoma is the most common and least aggressive (best-prognosis) thyroid cancer; anaplastic is the most aggressive (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 27. A diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism can be established by all of the following signs except: A. A negative reading on a Sulkowitch test. B. A serum calcium level of 12 mg/dL. C. An elevated level of parathyroid hormone. D. Bone demineralization seen on an x-ray film. Answer: A. A negative reading on a Sulkowitch test. Rationale: This is the 'except': hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia, so the Sulkowitch (urine calcium) test would be POSITIVE, not negative; elevated serum calcium, elevated PTH and bone demineralization all support the diagnosis (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 28. A recommended breakfast for a hyperparathyroid patient would be: A. Cereal with milk and bananas. B. Fried eggs and bacon. C. Orange juice and toast. D. Pork sausage and cranberry juice Answer: B. Fried eggs and bacon. Rationale: Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia, so a low-calcium breakfast is preferred; eggs and bacon avoid the high calcium of milk/cereal (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg nutrition guidance). Cereal with milk is high in calcium and thus inappropriate. 29. One of the most important and frequently occurring complications of hyperparathyroidism is: A. Kidney stones. B. Pancreatitis. C. Pathologic fractures. D. Peptic ulcer. Answer: A. Kidney stones. Rationale: Chronic hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria in hyperparathyroidism commonly cause renal calculi (nephrolithiasis) (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). Pathologic fractures occur but renal stones are the most frequent complication. 30. The pathophysiology of hypoparathyroidism is associated with all of the following except: A. A decrease in serum calcium. B. An elevation of blood phosphate. C. An increase in the renal excretion of phosphate. D. A lowered renal excretion of calcium. Answer: C. An increase in the renal excretion of phosphate. Rationale: This is the 'except': in hypoparathyroidism low PTH DECREASES renal phosphate excretion, causing hyperphosphatemia along with hypocalcemia and reduced renal calcium excretion (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 31. The goal of medical management for hypoparathyroidism is to: A. Achieve a serum calcium level of 9 to 10 mg/dL. B. Eliminate clinical symptoms. C. Reverse the symptoms of hypocalcemia. D. Accomplish all of the above. Answer: D. Accomplish all of the above. Rationale: Medical management of hypoparathyroidism aims to restore serum calcium to 9–10 mg/dL, reverse hypocalcemia and eliminate clinical symptoms (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg), so all listed goals apply. 32. Nursing management for a hypoparathyroid patient would not include: A. Maintaining a quiet, subdued environment. B. Making certain that calcium gluconate is kept at the bedside. C. Observing the patient for signs of tetany. D. Supplementing the diet with milk and milk products. Answer: D. Supplementing the diet with milk and milk products. Rationale: This is the 'would not include': milk products are high in phosphorus, which is already elevated in hypoparathyroidism, so a high-calcium/low-phosphorus diet is advised, not milk supplementation. Seizure precautions, bedside calcium gluconate and tetany monitoring are appropriate (Brunner & Suddarth's Med-Surg). 33. A pheochromocytoma is an adrenal medulla tumor that causes arterial hypertension by increasing the level of circulating: A. Catecholamines. B. Enzymes. C. Hormones. D. Glucocorticoids. Answer: A. Catecholamines. Rationale: Pheochromocytoma is an adrenal medulla tumor that secretes excess catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine), causing paroxysmal or sustained hypertension (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 34. A positive test for overactivity of the adrenal medulla is an epinephrine value of: A. 50 pg/mL. B. 100 pg/mL. C. 100 to 300 pg/mL. D. 450 pg/mL. Answer: D. 450 pg/mL. Rationale: Normal plasma epinephrine is under ~100 pg/mL; values above ~400 pg/mL indicate adrenal medulla overactivity (pheochromocytoma). 450 pg/mL is clearly elevated and positive (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 35. Laboratory findings suggestive of Addison's disease include all of the following except: A. A relative lymphocytosis. B. Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. C. Hypertension. D. Hypoglycemia. Answer: C. Hypertension. Rationale: Addison's disease (adrenal insufficiency) causes HYPOtension, not hypertension, due to aldosterone/cortisol deficiency. Expected findings are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia and relative lymphocytosis; hypertension is the exception (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 36. A positive diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome is associated with: A. The disappearance of lymphoid tissue. B. A reduction in circulating eosinophils. C. An elevated cortisol levels. D. All of the above. Answer: D. All of the above. Rationale: Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol) produces elevated cortisol levels, involution/disappearance of lymphoid tissue, and eosinopenia (reduced circulating eosinophils); all listed features apply (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 37. Clinical manifestations of Cushing's syndrome may be modified with a diet that is: A. High in protein. B. Low in carbohydrates. C. Low in sodium. D. All of the above. Answer: D. All of the above. Rationale: Cushing's manifestations are eased by a diet high in protein (counter catabolism), low in carbohydrates (counter hyperglycemia) and low in sodium (counter fluid retention/hypertension); all three apply (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 38. A patient with aldosteronism would be expected to exhibit all of the following symptoms except: A. Alkalosis. B. Hypokalemia. C. Hyponatremia. D. An increased pH. Answer: C. Hyponatremia. Rationale: Primary aldosteronism (excess aldosterone) causes sodium retention (HYPERnatremia), potassium loss (hypokalemia), and metabolic alkalosis with raised pH. Hyponatremia is the exception (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 39. The nurse needs to be aware that large-dose corticosteroid therapy is most effective when administered: A. At 8:00 AM. B. At 8:00 PM. C. Between 4:00 AM and 5:00 AM. D. Between 4:00 PM and 6:00 PM. Answer: A. At 8:00 AM. Rationale: Corticosteroids are best given in the early morning (around 8:00 AM) to mimic the body's natural diurnal cortisol peak and minimise HPA-axis suppression (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing; Kenya EML principles). 40. Nursing assessment for a patient who is receiving corticosteroid therapy includes observation for the unacceptable side effect of: A. Glaucoma. B. Facial mooning. C. Potassium loss. D. Weight gain Answer: A. Glaucoma. Rationale: Facial mooning, potassium loss and weight gain are expected/anticipated corticosteroid effects; glaucoma (raised intraocular pressure with possible vision loss) is a serious, unacceptable adverse effect requiring monitoring (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 41. Traumatic injury of the following section of spine causes acute respiratory failure: A. L1-L2 B. L3-L4 C. C5-C6 D. C7-C8 Answer: C. C5-C6 Rationale: The phrenic nerve (diaphragm) arises from C3-C5; high cervical injury at C5-C6 impairs diaphragmatic/respiratory function causing acute respiratory failure, whereas lumbar (L1-L4) injuries spare respiration (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 42. One of the following true about stomas: A. Healthy stomas are grey, bleed on touch, sensation on touch B. Colostomy bag should be emptied when full. C. Healthy stomas are pink, bleed on touch, has sensation on touch. D. It is yellow, bleeds on touch, there is no sensation on touch. Answer: C. Healthy stomas are pink, bleed on touch, has sensation on touch. Rationale: A healthy stoma is pink/red and moist, and slightly bleeds on touch because it is vascular. Note the stoma mucosa itself has no pain sensation; option C is the closest/best correct description among the choices (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 43. Barium swallow is used in diagnosis of the following: A. Jejunal atresia B. Stomach Cardia C. Upper GIT D. Rectal and Sigmoid tumors Answer: C. Upper GIT Rationale: A barium swallow outlines the upper gastrointestinal tract (pharynx, esophagus, stomach). Lower/rectosigmoid lesions require a barium enema, not a swallow (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 44. Chronic respiratory failure manifest with: A. p.H. =7.36, High PaCO2>50, and PaO2 <50 mmHg B. p.H. =7.56, High PaCO2>50, and PaO2 <50 mmHg C. p.H.7.37, High PaCO2<50, and PaO2 <50 mmHg D. PaO2 <50 mmHg, PaCO2 >50 mmHg, and pH =7.35 Answer: D. PaO2 <50 mmHg, PaCO2 >50 mmHg, and pH =7.35 Rationale: Chronic respiratory failure shows hypoxemia (PaO2 <50) and hypercapnia (PaCO2 >50) with a near-normal/compensated pH (~7.35) due to renal bicarbonate retention, unlike the acute uncompensated acidosis in the other options (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 45. Non atopic asthma is best described as: A. Start in adulthood. B. Associated with allergies. C. Patient with eczema is likely not to have it. D. Also known as intrinsic asthma. Answer: D. Also known as intrinsic asthma. Rationale: Non-atopic asthma is not associated with allergy/IgE and is termed intrinsic asthma; it typically starts in adulthood but the defining description is intrinsic (non-allergic) asthma (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 46. Failure of bone marrow results in: A. Pernicious anemia. B. Aplastic anemia with fever. C. Aplastic anemia without fever. D. Iron deficiency anemia. Answer: B. Aplastic anemia with fever. Rationale: Bone marrow failure causes aplastic anemia; because all cell lines fail (including neutrophils), leukopenia predisposes to infection and fever, distinguishing it from the febrile-free option (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 47. Hyperplasia of gingiva is likely to be indicator of: A. Ludwig angina B. Vincent angina C. Heart failure D. Phenytoin therapy Answer: D. Phenytoin therapy Rationale: Gingival hyperplasia is a classic adverse effect of phenytoin (anticonvulsant) therapy (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing; Kenya EML). 48. The bacteria known to cause dental caries is: A. Streptococcus aureas B. Streptococcus mutans C. Group A beta hemolytic streptococcus D. Sedenomonous aeruginosa Answer: B. Streptococcus mutans Rationale: Streptococcus mutans is the principal bacterium responsible for dental caries through acid production from fermentable carbohydrates (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing; standard microbiology). 49. Contralateral shift of trachea in patient with chest complains is likely to be due to: A. Pneumonia B. Emphysema C. Flail chest D. Tension pneumothorax Answer: D. Tension pneumothorax Rationale: Tension pneumothorax builds intrapleural pressure that pushes mediastinal structures and the trachea to the opposite (contralateral) side; it is a life-threatening emergency (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 50. Biot's respirations are associated with: A. Lesions on Pons. B. Diabetic ketoacidosis. C. Asthmatic attack. D. Pneumonia. Answer: A. Lesions on Pons. Rationale: Biot's (ataxic) respirations, an irregular pattern of breaths with apnea, are associated with damage to the pons/medulla (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). Kussmaul breathing, not Biot's, is seen in diabetic ketoacidosis. 51. ______is the deadliest form of gangrene: A. Wet gangrene B. Dry gangrene C. Gas gangrene D. Meleney's gangrene Answer: C. Gas gangrene Rationale: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis, usually Clostridium perfringens) is the deadliest, most rapidly fatal form of gangrene due to toxin production and systemic toxicity (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 52. Which of the following is unique to secondary venous thrombosis? A. It's usually without involvement of deep veins B. Its varicose veins: resulting from obstruction of deep veins. C. Its a reflux of venous blood in the veins D. It's usually managed by wearing static stockings. Answer: B. Its varicose veins: resulting from obstruction of deep veins. Rationale: Secondary varicose/venous disease is distinguished by an identifiable cause such as deep vein obstruction (e.g., prior DVT), unlike primary disease; this is the feature unique to secondary venous thrombosis among the options (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 53. The following is associated with thoracic aortic aneurysm only: A. Marfan syndrome B. Hypertension C. Atherosclerosis D. Smoking Answer: A. Marfan syndrome Rationale: Marfan syndrome (connective-tissue defect) is specifically linked to thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection, whereas hypertension, atherosclerosis and smoking are shared risk factors for abdominal aneurysms too (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 54. A burn obtained as a result of a lightning strike is: A. Heat burn B. Thermal burn C. Radiation burn D. Electrical burn Answer: D. Electrical burn Rationale: A lightning strike delivers a high-voltage electrical current, producing an electrical burn (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 55. In nursing assessment subjective data is data that the: A. Patient can report on their own B. Nurse can assess on their own C. Nurse and doctor can confirm D. Patient can report and the nurse can confirm Answer: A. Patient can report on their own Rationale: Subjective data is information reported by the patient (symptoms, feelings) that cannot be directly observed, whereas objective data is measurable/observable by the nurse (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing). 56. Damage to the mitral valve may lead: A. Pulmonary hypertension B. Left- sided heart failure C. Myocardial infarction D. Left ventricular hypertrophy Answer: A. Pulmonary hypertension Rationale: Mitral valve damage (stenosis/regurgitation) raises left atrial pressure that backs up into the pulmonary circulation, causing pulmonary hypertension (and later right heart strain) (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 57. One of the following procedures involves a segment of the leg being used to provide an alternative pathway for blood flow past a point of obstruction between the aorta and coronary artery: A. Angioplasty B. Coronary angiography C. Heart transplant D. Coronary bypass Answer: D. Coronary bypass Rationale: Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) uses a vessel such as the saphenous vein from the leg to bypass an obstruction and restore blood flow to the coronary artery (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 58. One of the following procedures involves using a small plastic balloon to open a narrowed artery: A. Heart transplant B. Coronary bypass C. Angioplasty D. Coronary angiography Answer: C. Angioplasty Rationale: Percutaneous transluminal (balloon) angioplasty uses a small inflatable balloon to open a narrowed artery (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 59. The most common symptom of myocardial infarction is: A. Palpitations B. Edema C. Dyspnea D. Chest pain Answer: D. Chest pain Rationale: Chest pain (crushing, substernal, possibly radiating) is the most common presenting symptom of myocardial infarction (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 60. Dyspnea, fatigue, increased pulmonary artery pressure and decreased cardiac output are indicative of: A. Right valve failure B. Paracentisis C. Myocardial infarction D. Left sided heart failure Answer: D. Left sided heart failure Rationale: Dyspnea, fatigue, raised pulmonary artery pressure and reduced cardiac output reflect left-sided heart failure, where the failing left ventricle causes pulmonary congestion and low output (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 61. The primary reason for administration of morphine in a patient with myocardial infarction is to relieve: A. Edema B. Palpitations C. Chest pain D. Dyspnea Answer: C. Chest pain Rationale: In myocardial infarction, morphine is given primarily to relieve severe ischemic chest pain (and also reduces anxiety and cardiac workload/preload) (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing; Kenya EML). 62. Which diagnostic test provides information about the physiology and function of the heart? A. Electrocardiogram B. Chest X-ray C. Echocardiogram D. Angiogram Answer: A. Electrocardiogram Rationale: The electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart's electrical activity, giving information about cardiac physiology and function (rate, rhythm, conduction, ischemia), whereas echocardiogram shows structure/mechanics and X-ray shows size (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 63. One of the following conditions results in coronary artery disease: A. Renal failure B. Diabetes mellitus C. Myocardial infarction D. Atherosclerosis Answer: D. Atherosclerosis Rationale: Atherosclerosis (plaque buildup narrowing coronary arteries) is the underlying pathological process that directly results in coronary artery disease (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 64. Nursing diagnoses mostly differ from medical diagnoses in that they are: A. Primarily concerned with human response, while medical diagnoses are primarily concerned with pathology B. Dependent upon medical diagnoses for the direction of appropriate interventions C. Primarily concerned with caring, while medical diagnoses are primarily concerned with curing D. Primarily concerned with psychosocial parameters, while medical diagnoses are primarily concerned with physiologic parameters. Answer: A. Primarily concerned with human response, while medical diagnoses are primarily concerned with pathology Rationale: A nursing diagnosis addresses the patient's human responses to actual/potential health problems, whereas a medical diagnosis identifies the disease/pathology (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing). 65. In the management of myocardial infarction, atherectomy is: A. Removal of atherosclerotic plaque B. Use of new implants C. Ballooning of narrowed artery D. Putting a stent to prevent collapse of artery) Answer: A. Removal of atherosclerotic plaque Rationale: Atherectomy is a catheter-based procedure that cuts away/removes atherosclerotic plaque from the coronary artery wall, distinct from angioplasty (ballooning) or stenting (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing, cardiovascular interventions). 66. The nursing diagnosis for a patient with angina pectoris is infective tissue perfusion. The plan of care includes the patient outcome criterion of: A. Experiencing no dyspnea on exertion B. Reduce ischemia by increasing O2 to tissues C. Agreeing to discontinue smoking D. Ambulating 50 feet without experiencing dyspnea Answer: D. Ambulating 50 feet without experiencing dyspnea Rationale: An outcome criterion must be patient-centred, measurable and observable. 'Ambulating 50 feet without dyspnea' is a specific, measurable patient outcome; the others are goals/interventions rather than measurable outcome criteria (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing, nursing process). 67. Which diagnostic test will be used to test for claudication in peripheral artery disease? A. Doppler ultrasound B. Treadmill C. Arteriogram D. Ankle brachial index Answer: D. Ankle brachial index Rationale: The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the primary, first-line diagnostic test for peripheral artery disease/claudication, quantifying arterial insufficiency of the lower limbs (Brunner & Suddarth's, peripheral vascular assessment). 68. Which of the following cardiovascular condition is more prevalent among females than males: A. Hypertension B. Varicose veins C. Coronary artery disease D. Myocardial infarction Answer: B. Varicose veins Rationale: Varicose veins are more prevalent in females (pregnancy, hormonal influence), whereas coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction are more common in males (Brunner & Suddarth's, venous disorders). 69. Which action occurs primarily during the evaluation phase of the nursing process: A. Decision making and judgment B. Data collection C. Reassessment and audit D. Priority setting and expected outcomes. Answer: C. Reassessment and audit Rationale: The evaluation phase of the nursing process involves reassessing the patient and auditing whether outcomes were met. Data collection is assessment; priority setting/expected outcomes are planning; decision making is diagnosis (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing). 70. Cognitive skills, key in implementation of nursing process, refers to: A. A blend of intellectual and 'hand' on skills B. 'Hands on' skills such as manipulating equipment C. Problem solving, decision making, critical thinking and curative thinking D. All activities, verbal and nonverbal, that people use when communicating directly with one another Answer: C. Problem solving, decision making, critical thinking and curative thinking Rationale: Cognitive (intellectual) skills in the nursing process refer to problem solving, decision making and critical thinking. Option B describes psychomotor skills and D describes interpersonal skills (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing, implementation). 71. Hematocrit of 60% is likely to be an indicator of: A. Leukemia B. Idiopathic Thrombocytopenia. C. Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma D. Polycythemia vera Answer: D. Polycythemia vera Rationale: A markedly elevated hematocrit (60%) indicates an increased red cell mass, characteristic of polycythemia vera. Leukemia, ITP and lymphoma do not raise the hematocrit (Brunner & Suddarth's, hematologic disorders). 72. A patient with Forced Expiratory Volume (FEV1) of 60% is likely to be suffering from: A. Pleural effusion. B. Trauma. C. Emphysema. D. Asthma. Answer: C. Emphysema. Rationale: A reduced FEV1 (60%) with airflow obstruction is characteristic of COPD/emphysema, an obstructive lung disease. Pleural effusion is restrictive; emphysema best fits chronic obstruction (Brunner & Suddarth's, respiratory function tests). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 73. Vitamin B12 anemia is characterized by: A. Microcytosis of RBC B. Normal hematocrit C. Hypochromic RBC D. Macrocytosis of RBC Answer: D. Macrocytosis of RBC Rationale: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia characterized by large red cells (macrocytosis) with high MCV, not microcytosis or hypochromia (Brunner & Suddarth's, anemias). 74. One following oxygen delivery system has constant FiO2: A. Nasal Prongs B. Venturi Mask C. Non-rebreather mask D. Partial rebreather mask Answer: B. Venturi Mask Rationale: The Venturi mask is a high-flow device that delivers a precise, constant FiO2 regardless of the patient's breathing pattern; nasal prongs and rebreather masks deliver variable FiO2 (Brunner & Suddarth's, oxygen therapy). 75. Patient manifesting with "hot potato voice" is likely to be suffering from: A. Vincent angina B. Periodontitis C. Asthma D. Ludwig Angina Answer: D. Ludwig Angina Rationale: A muffled 'hot potato voice' results from the pharyngeal/submandibular swelling of Ludwig's angina (and severe peritonsillar/deep neck infection); it is not a feature of asthma or periodontitis (Brunner & Suddarth's, upper airway infections). 76. The nursing action needed for claustrophobic patient before MRI is: A. Explain the procedure to the patient. B. Assume patient's concerns C. Give paralytic drugs to the patient. D. Tell the patient to man up. Answer: A. Explain the procedure to the patient. Rationale: For a claustrophobic patient facing MRI, the nurse should first explain the procedure to reduce anxiety and gain cooperation; assuming concerns or dismissive/inappropriate responses are non-therapeutic (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing, therapeutic communication). 77. The best imaging study for patient with basilar artery aneurysm is: A. Magnetic resonance imaging B. X-Ray C. Coronary angiography D. Radioisotope imaging Answer: A. Magnetic resonance imaging Rationale: MRI (with MR angiography) is the preferred non-invasive imaging for cerebral/basilar artery aneurysms; plain X-ray and coronary angiography are unsuitable for intracranial vessels (Brunner & Suddarth's, neurologic diagnostics). 78. Mild intermittent asthma is best managed by: A. Long-acting beta-adrenergic agonist (LABA) B. Short acting beta-adrenergic agonist (SABA) C. Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) D. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) Answer: B. Short acting beta-adrenergic agonist (SABA) Rationale: Mild intermittent asthma is managed with a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) as reliever therapy; ICS and LABA/LAMA are for persistent asthma (GINA/WHO guidance as adopted in Kenya, Brunner & Suddarth's). 79. X-ray film of a patient shows expanded airways. This likely to be indicative of: A. Emphysema B. Bronchiectasis C. Tension pneumothorax D. Diffused pneumonia Answer: A. Emphysema Rationale: Emphysema causes hyperinflation with expanded/enlarged airspaces and flattened diaphragm on chest X-ray; tension pneumothorax shows lung collapse, not expanded airways (Brunner & Suddarth's, COPD). 80. Hemoptysis is defined as: A. Blood in sputum cough. B. Blood in GIT C. Bad breath D. Dry cough Answer: A. Blood in sputum cough. Rationale: Hemoptysis is the coughing up of blood or blood-stained sputum from the respiratory tract; blood in the GIT is hematemesis/melena (Brunner & Suddarth's, respiratory assessment). 81. One of the following is an Intracardiac shunt A. Ductus arteriosus B. Ductus venosus C. Foramen ovale D. Ostia of aorta Answer: C. Foramen ovale Rationale: The foramen ovale is an intracardiac shunt between the right and left atria in fetal circulation; the ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus are extracardiac shunts (Guyton/standard physiology; fetal circulation). 82. The immediate drainage of left intercostal veins is____________ A. Internal thoracic vein B. Azygous vein C. Hemiazagous vein D. Inferior venacava Answer: C. Hemiazagous vein Rationale: The left (lower) posterior intercostal veins drain immediately into the hemiazygos vein, which then crosses to the azygos vein; the right side drains to the azygos (standard anatomy, venous drainage of the thorax). 83. The cerebral vessels, CSF, and the cranial nerves are found within____________space. A. Subdural B. Epidural C. Subarachnoid D. Beneath Pia matter Answer: C. Subarachnoid Rationale: The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the cerebral vessels and the cranial nerves as they traverse it; the subdural and epidural spaces are potential spaces (standard neuroanatomy). 84. One of the following will reduce pulse of pressure of an individual: A. Reduced osmolality B. Dehydration C. Highly hydration status D. Low temperatures Answer: B. Dehydration Rationale: Pulse pressure is stroke volume dependent; dehydration/hypovolemia reduces stroke volume and thus narrows the pulse pressure. Overhydration would widen it (Guyton physiology; Brunner & Suddarth's, fluid balance). 85. Sensory neurons enter the spinal cord via: A. Lateral horn B. Anterior horn C. Central canal D. Posterior horn Answer: D. Posterior horn Rationale: Sensory (afferent) neurons enter the spinal cord via the dorsal (posterior) root and synapse in the posterior/dorsal horn; motor neurons exit via the anterior horn (standard neuroanatomy). 86. The following conductive system of the heart fire action potential at higher frequency than the rest: A. Sino Atrio Node B. Atrioventricular Node C. Bundle of His D. Purkinje fibers Answer: A. Sino Atrio Node Rationale: The sinoatrial (SA) node has the fastest intrinsic firing rate (~60-100/min) and thus acts as the natural pacemaker; the AV node, Bundle of His and Purkinje fibers fire at progressively lower rates (Guyton physiology; cardiac conduction). 87. The anterior 2/3 of tongue is innervated by cranial nerve: A. 1 B. 3 C. 5 D. 7 Answer: D. 7 Rationale: General sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual (V3) nerve, but taste is carried by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII); among the options 7 (facial) is correct for taste innervation (standard neuroanatomy). 88. Spinal cord terminates at: A. T12-L1 B. T11-T12 C. L1-L2 D. L4-L5 Answer: C. L1-L2 Rationale: In adults the spinal cord terminates as the conus medullaris at the L1-L2 vertebral level; below this is the cauda equina (standard neuroanatomy). 89. Phrenic nerve is formed by following spinal cord plexus: A. Cervical plexus B. Lumber plexus C. Thoracic nerves D. Sacral plexus Answer: A. Cervical plexus Rationale: The phrenic nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C3, C4, C5) and supplies the diaphragm (standard anatomy, cervical plexus). 90. One of the following is true about renal system: A. Renal artery carries purified blood. B. Renal vein carries oxygenated blood. C. Renal vein carries blood with metabolic wastes. D. It participates in erythropoiesis Answer: D. It participates in erythropoiesis Rationale: The kidney produces erythropoietin and thus participates in erythropoiesis. The renal artery carries oxygenated (not purified) blood and the renal vein carries deoxygenated, filtered blood, making the other options false (Guyton physiology; renal function). 91. One of the following wave represent atrial depolarization: A. P B. Q C. R D. T Answer: A. P Rationale: The P wave of the ECG represents atrial depolarization; the QRS represents ventricular depolarization and the T wave ventricular repolarization (Brunner & Suddarth's, ECG interpretation). 92. The following parts of central nervous system control vegetative function: A. Spinal cord B. Cerebral cortex C. Brain stem D. Medulla oblongata Answer: D. Medulla oblongata Rationale: The medulla oblongata houses the vital autonomic (vegetative) centres controlling cardiac, respiratory and vasomotor function; it is the most specific answer among the options (standard neuroanatomy/physiology). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 93. The occipital lobe of brain: A. Concerned with olfaction B. Concerned with sense of test C. Control osmolality D. Concerned with vision. Answer: D. Concerned with vision. Rationale: The occipital lobe contains the primary visual cortex and is concerned with vision; olfaction and taste are processed elsewhere (standard neuroanatomy). 94. One of following is a nerve formed by brachial plexus: A. Radial nerve B. Tibial nerve C. Sciatic nerve D. Pudendal nerve Answer: A. Radial nerve Rationale: The radial nerve is a branch of the brachial plexus supplying the upper limb; the tibial, sciatic and pudendal nerves arise from the lumbosacral plexus (standard anatomy, brachial plexus). 95. The fibers that pass through the internal capsule form: A. Pyramidal tracts B. Extrapyramidal tract C. Rubrospinal tract D. Cranial nerves Answer: A. Pyramidal tracts Rationale: The corticospinal (pyramidal) tract fibers descend through the posterior limb of the internal capsule; the extrapyramidal and rubrospinal tracts take other routes (standard neuroanatomy, motor pathways). 96. The following cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye: A. 1 B. 3 C. 5 D. 6 Answer: D. 6 Rationale: The abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye (standard neuroanatomy, cranial nerves). 97. Collection of cell bodies in the central nervous system forms: A. White matter B. Grey matter C. Commissures D. Ganglion Answer: B. Grey matter Rationale: Per standard neuroanatomy (Kozier & Erb's / Brunner & Suddarth), collections of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS form grey matter, whereas myelinated axons form white matter and a cluster of cell bodies OUTSIDE the CNS is a ganglion. 98. Gonadal arteries branch from: A. Internal iliac artery B. External iliac artery C. Abdominal aorta D. Subclavian artery Answer: C. Abdominal aorta Rationale: Per standard anatomy (Gray's/anatomy texts used in Kenyan training), the gonadal (testicular/ovarian) arteries arise directly from the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries, not from the iliac or subclavian vessels. 99. Foamy and greasy stool is a likely indicator of: A. Secretory Diarrhea B. Celiac disease C. Upper GI bleeding D. Steatorrhea Answer: D. Steatorrhea Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, foamy, greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stool that reflects fat malabsorption is by definition steatorrhea; celiac disease can cause it but the descriptive finding itself IS steatorrhea. 100. Esophageal varices are caused by: A. GERD B. Peptic ulcers C. Cirrhosis D. Hemorrhoids Answer: C. Cirrhosis Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, oesophageal varices result from portal hypertension, most commonly caused by hepatic cirrhosis, which raises portal venous pressure and dilates the oesophageal collateral veins. 101. The following gastrointestinal disorder is managed best by downscaling wheat product in diet A. Irritable bowel syndrome B. Diverticulum C. Celiac disease D. Esophageal varices. Answer: C. Celiac disease Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, celiac disease is gluten-sensitive enteropathy; management centres on a gluten-free diet, i.e. eliminating wheat, barley and rye products. 102. One of the following disorder is caused by increased tone of lower esophageal sphincter: A. GERD B. Achalasia C. Hiatal hernia D. Dumping syndrome Answer: B. Achalasia Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, achalasia is characterised by increased tone / failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, whereas GERD and hiatal hernia involve a weak/incompetent LES. 103. Oliguria in renal function means: A. Urine output of < 250 mL /24 hours B. Urine output of <1000 mL /24 hours C. Urine output of < 2500 mL /24 hours D. Urine output of < 500 mL /24 hours Answer: D. Urine output of < 500 mL /24 hours Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth and standard renal physiology, oliguria is defined as urine output less than 500 mL in 24 hours (or <0.5 mL/kg/hr); <100 mL/24 hr is anuria. 104. Normal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is_________ mL /min/m2 and above. A. 30 B. 40 C. 50 D. 60 Answer: D. 60 Rationale: Per KDIGO/standard renal references used in Kenyan practice, a normal GFR is ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (typically 90–120); values below 60 sustained ≥3 months indicate chronic kidney disease. 105. Urine specific gravity of 1.100 is indicative of: A. Normal hydration B. Fluid overload C. Dehydration D. None of the above Answer: C. Dehydration Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, a high urine specific gravity indicates concentrated urine seen in dehydration/fluid volume deficit (normal range ~1.005–1.030); a very high value reflects reduced water intake and haemoconcentration. 106. One of the following is inappropriate health education to a discharge patient with chronic kidney disease. A. Use NSAID to manage mild pain. B. Reduce red meat intake and increase carbohydrates C. Reduce dietary intake of salt intake. D. Reduce dietary intake of potassium. Answer: A. Use NSAID to manage mild pain. Rationale: Per Kenya MOH renal/CKD guidance and Brunner & Suddarth, NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and contraindicated in CKD, so advising their use is INAPPROPRIATE education; salt, potassium and protein restriction are appropriate. 107. Management of moderately elevated K+ in a patient with acute kidney injury involve the following: A. Administration of KCl by slow infusion B. Administration of spironolactone to aid elimination. C. Administration of insulin to aid in redistribution D. None of the above Answer: C. Administration of insulin to aid in redistribution Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth and MOH emergency guidance, IV insulin (with dextrose) shifts potassium intracellularly to lower serum K+; giving KCl would worsen it and spironolactone (K-sparing) is contraindicated in hyperkalaemia/AKI. 108. Nephrotic syndrome is manifested by one of the following: A. Proteinuria, Hypoalbuminemia, Edema, Hyperlipidemia. B. Hyperkalemia, Hyperalbuminemia, Edema, Hypertension C. Proteinuria, Hypoalbuminemia, Edema, Hypokalemia D. Proteinuria, Hyperalbuminemia, Edema, Hyperlipidemia. Answer: A. Proteinuria, Hypoalbuminemia, Edema, Hyperlipidemia. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, the classic tetrad of nephrotic syndrome is massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. 109. One of the following is likely to cause urolithiasis A. Hypertension B. Diabetes insipidus C. Hyperparathyroidism D. Compulsive water intake Answer: C. Hyperparathyroidism Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, hyperparathyroidism raises serum calcium and urinary calcium excretion, predisposing to calcium-containing renal stones (urolithiasis); compulsive water intake is protective. 110. The most common kidney stones are: A. Calcium Phosphate salts. B. Uric acid and Struvite C. Calcium Oxalate D. Amino acid Cystine Answer: C. Calcium Oxalate Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of kidney stone (about 75–80% of cases). 111. Lesion of cranial nerve VII causes one of the following: A. Ebbs palsy B. Inability to raise neck C. Bell's Palsy D. Anosmia Answer: C. Bell's Palsy Rationale: Per standard neuroanatomy (Brunner & Suddarth), the facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression; its lesion causes Bell's palsy (unilateral facial droop). Anosmia is CN I; CN VII does not affect neck raising. 112. Which one of the following combinations of antiparkinsonian drugs is an appropriate treatment plan? A. Amantadine, carbidopa, and entacapone. B. Levodopa, carbidopa, and entacapone. C. Pramipexole, carbidopa, and entacapone. D. Ropinirole, carbidopa, and selegiline. Answer: B. Levodopa, carbidopa, and entacapone. Rationale: Per Kenya EML/pharmacology texts, the standard Parkinson's regimen combines levodopa (dopamine precursor) with carbidopa (peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor) and entacapone (COMT inhibitor); the other options pair carbidopa with drugs (amantadine, dopamine agonists) that are not levodopa and so gain no benefit from carbidopa. 113. Carbidopa used as antiparkinsonian drug is a: A. Dopamine receptor agonist B. Decarboxylase inhibitor C. Catechol-o-methyl transferase inhibitor D. Monoamine oxidase B inhibitor Answer: B. Decarboxylase inhibitor Rationale: Per standard pharmacology, carbidopa is a peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor that prevents peripheral conversion of levodopa, increasing CNS availability and reducing peripheral side effects. 114. The part of brain affected in parkinsonian disease is the: A. Limbic system B. Occipital lobe C. Pyramidal tracts D. Basal ganglia Answer: D. Basal ganglia Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the basal ganglia, impairing control of voluntary movement. 115. One of the following is a rapidly progressing, ascending inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy of the peripheral sensory and motor nerves and nerve roots disease. A. Myasthenia Gravis B. Guillain-Barre Syndrome C. Multiple Myeloma D. Alzheimer's disease Answer: B. Guillain-Barre Syndrome Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute, rapidly progressive ascending inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy affecting peripheral sensory and motor nerves and nerve roots. 116. The following is a cutoff for diagnosis of increased intracranial pressure (ICP): A. ICP of 5 mmHg B. ICP of 10 mmHg C. ICP of 15 mmHg D. ICP of 20 mmHg Answer: D. ICP of 20 mmHg Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth and standard neuro-critical care, normal ICP is 5–15 mmHg; a sustained ICP above 20 mmHg is the threshold defining raised intracranial pressure requiring treatment. Source: FQE Paper 2 — KRCHN Diploma (June 2024) 117. A postpartum patient was in labor for 30 hours and had ruptured membranes for 24 hours. For which of the following would the nurse be alert? A. Endometritis B. Endometriosis C. Salpingitis D. Pelvic thrombophlebitis Answer: A. Endometritis Rationale: Prolonged labor with prolonged rupture of membranes (>18-24h) allows ascending bacteria to infect the uterine lining, so the nurse watches for endometritis (puerperal infection). Endometriosis and salpingitis are unrelated to this postpartum risk. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (puerperal sepsis). 118. When caring for a 3-day-old neonate who is receiving phototherapy to treat jaundice, the nurse in charge would expect to do which of the following? A. Turn the neonate every 6 hours B. Encourage the mother to discontinue breastfeeding C. Notify the physician if the skin becomes bronze D. Check the vital signs every 2 to 4 hours Answer: D. Check the vital signs every 2 to 4 hours Rationale: During phototherapy the neonate can become hyperthermic/dehydrated, so vital signs are monitored every 2-4 hours; breastfeeding is continued and bronze skin (bronze-baby syndrome) is documented, not primarily reported. Per Basic Paediatric Protocols (Kenya) neonatal jaundice management. 119. The nurse is caring for a primigravida at about 2 months and 1-week gestation. After explaining self-care measures for common discomforts of pregnancy, the nurse determines that the client understands the instructions when she says: A. “Nausea and vomiting can be reduced if I eat a few crackers before rising” B. “If I start to leak colostrum, I should cleanse my nipples with soap and water.” C. “If I have a vaginal discharge, I should wear nylon underwear.” D. “Leg cramps can be alleviated if I put an ice pack on the area.” Answer: A. “Nausea and vomiting can be reduced if I eat a few crackers before rising” Rationale: Eating dry crackers before rising is the correct self-care for morning nausea. Nipples should be washed with water only (soap dries them), cotton (not nylon) underwear is advised, and leg cramps are relieved by dorsiflexion/warmth, not ice. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (minor disorders of pregnancy). 120. A pregnant client is diagnosed with partial placenta previa. In explaining the diagnosis, the nurse tells the client that the usual treatment for partial placenta previa is which of the following? A. Activity limited to bed rest B. Platelet infusion C. Immediate cesarean delivery D. Labor induction with oxytocin. Answer: A. Activity limited to bed rest Rationale: In stable partial placenta previa without active heavy bleeding, expectant management with bed rest is standard to prolong gestation; cesarean is reserved for term or uncontrolled bleeding, and oxytocin induction is contraindicated. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives / MOH maternal guidelines. 121. The nurse plans to instruct the postpartum client about methods to prevent breast engorgement. Which of the following measures would the nurse include in the teaching plan? A. Feeding the neonate a maximum of 5 minutes per side on the first day B. Wearing a supportive brassiere with nipple shields C. Breastfeeding the neonate at frequent intervals D. Decreasing fluid intake for the first 24 to 48 hours Answer: C. Breastfeeding the neonate at frequent intervals Rationale: Frequent breastfeeding empties the breasts and prevents engorgement; time-limited feeds, restricting fluids, and nipple shields do not prevent engorgement. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives / MOH breastfeeding guidelines. 122. When the nurse on duty accidentally bumps the bassinet, the neonate throws out its arms, hands open, and begins to cry. The nurse interprets this reaction as indicative of which of the following reflexes? A. Startle reflex B. Babinski reflex C. Grasping reflex D. Tonic neck reflex Answer: A. Startle reflex Rationale: Sudden jarring causing symmetrical arm abduction with open hands followed by crying is the Moro (startle) reflex. Babinski is toe fanning to sole stroking, grasp is finger curling, and tonic neck is the fencing posture. Per Kozier & Erb / Basic Paediatric Protocols (newborn assessment). 123. A primigravida client at 25 weeks gestation visits the clinic and tells the nurse that her lower back aches when she arrives home from work. The nurse should suggest that the client perform: A. Tailor sitting B. Leg lifting C. Shoulder circling D. Squatting exercises Answer: A. Tailor sitting Rationale: Tailor (cross-legged) sitting strengthens the back and stretches pelvic muscles, relieving low backache in pregnancy. Leg lifting and squatting can strain the back; shoulder circling targets the upper body. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (antenatal exercises). 124. Which of the following would the nurse most likely expect to find when assessing a pregnant client with abruption placenta? A. Excessive vaginal bleeding B. Rigid, board-like abdomen C. Tetanic uterine contractions D. Premature rupture of membranes Answer: B. Rigid, board-like abdomen Rationale: Abruptio placentae classically causes a rigid, board-like, tender abdomen from concealed retroplacental bleeding; vaginal bleeding may be minimal/concealed. Excessive painless bleeding suggests previa. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives / MOH obstetric guidelines. 125. A client tells the nurse, “I think my baby likes to hear me talk to him.” When discussing neonates and stimulation with sound, which of the following would the nurse include as a means to elicit the best response? A. High-pitched speech with tonal variations B. Low-pitched speech with a sameness of tone C. Cooing sounds rather than words D. Repeated stimulation with loud sounds Answer: A. High-pitched speech with tonal variations Rationale: Neonates respond best to high-pitched speech with tonal variation (infant-directed speech), which promotes attention and bonding. Loud sounds and monotone are less effective. Per Kozier & Erb / developmental care principles. 126. A patient in her 14th week of pregnancy has presented with abdominal cramping and vaginal bleeding for the past 8 hours. She has passed several clots. What is the primary nursing diagnosis for this patient? A. Knowledge deficit B. Fluid volume deficit C. Anticipatory grieving D. Pain Answer: B. Fluid volume deficit Rationale: With active vaginal bleeding, clot passage and cramping (inevitable/incomplete abortion), the priority (physiologic, ABC) nursing diagnosis is fluid volume deficit; grieving and pain follow once the patient is stabilized. Per Kozier & Erb prioritization / Myles. 127. A primigravida patient is admitted to the labor delivery area. Assessment reveals that she is in the early part of the first stage of labor. Her pain is likely to be most intense: A. Around the pelvic girdle B. Around the pelvic girdle and in the upper arms C. Around the pelvic girdle and at the perineum D. At the perineum Answer: A. Around the pelvic girdle Rationale: In the early first stage, pain from cervical dilatation is referred to the lower abdomen and pelvic girdle (T10-L1). Perineal pain arises in the second stage. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (physiology of labor pain). 128. A female adult patient is taking a progestin-only oral contraceptive or mini pill. Progestin use may increase the patient’s risk for: A. Endometriosis B. Female hypogonadism C. Premenstrual syndrome D. Tubal or ectopic pregnancy Answer: D. Tubal or ectopic pregnancy Rationale: Progestin-only pills slow tubal motility, so if failure occurs the pregnancy is more likely to be ectopic; progestins do not cause endometriosis, hypogonadism, or PMS. Per Kenya National Family Planning Guidelines / BNF. 129. A patient with pregnancy-induced hypertension probably exhibits which of the following symptoms? A. Proteinuria, headaches, vaginal bleeding B. Headaches, double vision, vaginal bleeding C. Proteinuria, headaches, double vision D. Proteinuria, double vision, uterine contractions Answer: C. Proteinuria, headaches, double vision Rationale: Preeclampsia/PIH presents with proteinuria, headache, and visual disturbances (double/blurred vision) from cerebral/retinal involvement; vaginal bleeding is not a feature. Per MOH/WHO pre-eclampsia guidelines and Myles. 130. The nurse in charge is caring for a patient who is in the first stage of labor. What is the shortest but most difficult part of this stage? A. Active phase B. Complete phase C. Latent phase D. Transitional phase Answer: D. Transitional phase Rationale: The transitional phase (8-10 cm) is the shortest but most intense and difficult part of the first stage of labor. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (stages of labor). 131. The nurse is developing a teaching plan for a patient who is 8 weeks pregnant. The nurse should tell the patient that she can expect to feel the fetus move at which time? A. Between 10 and 12 weeks’ gestation B. Between 16 and 20 weeks’ gestation C. Between 21 and 23 weeks’ gestation D. Between 24 and 26 weeks’ gestation Answer: B. Between 16 and 20 weeks’ gestation Rationale: Quickening (first felt fetal movement) typically occurs at 16-20 weeks in a primigravida. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (presumptive signs of pregnancy). 132. Normal lochial findings in the first 24 hours post-delivery include: A. Bright red blood B. Large clots or tissue fragments C. A foul odor D. The complete absence of lochia Answer: A. Bright red blood Rationale: Lochia rubra (bright red blood) is normal in the first 1-3 days postpartum. Large clots/tissue, foul odor, and absence of lochia are abnormal. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (puerperium). 133. Accompanied by her husband, a patient seeks admission to the labor and delivery area. The client states that she is in labor and says she attended the hospital clinic for prenatal care. Which question should the nurse ask her first? A. “Do you have any chronic illness?” B. “Do you have any allergies?” C. “What is your expected due date?” D. “Who will be with you during labor?” Answer: C. “What is your expected due date?” Rationale: On admission in labor the immediate priority is to establish gestational age via the expected due date to guide management; allergies and history follow. Per Myles Textbook for Midwives (admission in labor). 134. A patient is in the second stage of labor. During this stage, how frequently should the nurse in charge assess her uterine contractions? A. Every 5 minutes B. Every 15 minutes C. Every 30 minutes D. Every 60 minutes Answer: B. Every 15 minutes Rationale: In the second stage of labor, uterine contractions and fetal heart are assessed at least every 15 minutes (FHR every 5 min in high-risk). Per WHO/MOH intrapartum monitoring and Myles. 135. A patient is in her last trimester of pregnancy. Nurse Vickie should instruct her to notify her primary health care provider immediately if she notices: A. Blurred vision B. Hemorrhoids C. Increased vaginal mucus D. Shortness of breath on exertion Answer: A. Rubella exposure is teratogenic (not genetic) and preterm labor is obstetric history. Per Myles / genetics in midwifery. 137. An adult female patient is using the rhythm (calendar-basal body temperature) method of family planning. In this method, the unsafe period for sexual intercourse is indicated by: A. C. 3 full days of elevated basal body temperature and clear, thin cervical mucus D. Per Kenya National Family Planning Guidelines. 138. The nurse is caring for a client in labor. The external fetal monitor shows a pattern of variable decelerations in fetal heart rate. Cesarean is a later step if the pattern persists. Per WHO/MOH intrapartum guidelines and Myles. 139. Which of the following would be a disadvantage of breastfeeding? A. Involution occurs more rapidly B. The incidence of allergies increases due to maternal antibodies C. Which of the following would cause a false-positive result on a pregnancy test? A. The test was performed less than 10 days after an abortion B. Which of the following characteristics of contractions would the nurse expect to find in a client experiencing true labor? A. Occurring at irregular intervals B. Starting mainly in the abdomen C. During which of the following stages of labor would the nurse assess “crowning”? A. First stage B. Second stage C. Third stage D. Fourth stage Answer: B. Second stage Rationale: Crowning (the fetal head remaining visible at the vulva between contractions) occurs in the second stage of labour, the stage of expulsion (Myles Textbook for Midwives). 153. The other actions relate to airway, scoring and cord, not thermoregulation. 155. Immediately before expulsion, which of the following cardinal movements occur? A. Descent B. Flexion C. Extension D. Before birth, which of the following structures connects the right and left auricles of the heart? A. Umbilical vein B. Foramen ovale C. Ductus arteriosus D. Ductus venosus Answer: B. Foramen ovale Rationale: The foramen ovale is the fetal shunt in the interatrial septum allowing blood to pass from the right to the left atrium (auricles) bypassing the lungs. When assessing the newborn’s heart rate, which of the following ranges would be considered normal if the newborn were sleeping? Which of the following is true regarding the fontanels of the newborn? A. The anterior is triangular shaped; the posterior is diamond-shaped B. In which of the following types of spontaneous abortions would the nurse assess dark brown vaginal discharge and a negative pregnancy test? A. Threatened B. Imminent C. Missed D. Which of the following sign may help a midwife diagnose shoulder dystocia in labour ward? A. The fetal head remains slightly stuck in the vagina B. During vacuum extraction procedure, the centre of the vacuum cup should be placed over which of the flexion point on the fetal head? A. Deficient fluid volume Rationale: Per Basic Paediatric Protocols and nursing care standards, phototherapy increases insensible water loss and stool water, so deficient fluid volume (risk of dehydration) is the priority; skin integrity and thermoregulation are managed but fluid loss is the leading concern. 203. Radiation refers to: A. loss of heat through water evaporation from the baby B. loss of heat through the baby shivering C. loss of heat from the baby's surface to surrounding colder objects D. loss of heat to moving air or fluid around the baby Answer: C. loss of heat from the baby's surface to surrounding colder objects Rationale: Radiation is heat transfer from the newborn's body surface to nearby cooler solid objects not in direct contact (e.g. cold walls/windows). Evaporation is water loss, convection is loss to moving air, conduction is loss to objects in contact. Per Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols / Myles (thermoregulation). 220. The body and the extremities are pale Rationale: An Apgar of 0/1 indicates a severely depressed neonate; only the completely pale/absent colour (0 for colour, no cyanosis grading possible) fits. The nurse prepares to administer a phytonadione (vitamin K) injection to a newborn, which explanation should the nurse give to the mother concerning the medication? Which one of the following is an uncontrollable risk factor that has been linked to development of coronary artery disease(CAD) A. A 21 year old male client is transported by ambulance to the emergency unit. He complains of severe pain in his right chest where he struck the steering wheel. Which is the primary client goal at this time? A. Reduce client’s anxiety B. Maintain adequate oxygenation C. Decrease chest pain D. Maintain adequate circulating volume Answer: B. Maintain adequate oxygenation Rationale: With blunt chest trauma the ABC priority (airway/breathing) makes maintaining adequate oxygenation the primary goal; Brunner & Suddarth trauma management places oxygenation before pain and anxiety control. 261. The following are risk factors for impaired gas exchange and pulmonary infection : A. Immobility, constipation and incontinence B. Fluid restriction, immunosuppression and decreased level of consciousness. C. Fluid restriction, immobility and ingestion of seasoned foods D. Incontinence, chemotherapy and anemia Answer: B. Fluid restriction, immunosuppression and decreased level of consciousness. Rationale: Fluid restriction thickens secretions, immunosuppression predisposes to infection, and decreased LOC impairs airway clearance/cough — all promoting impaired gas exchange and pulmonary infection (Brunner & Suddarth respiratory nursing). 262. When nursing a patient on steroids, the nurse should, A. Observe for oedema, weigh daily, monitor blood counts B. Maintain infection control, monitor blood sugar, maintain hydration C. Observe for bone marrow suppression, minimise exposure to heat,encourage bed rest D. Encourage increased fluid intake, administer anti-emetics, monitor RBC count Answer: B. Maintain infection control, monitor blood sugar, maintain hydration Rationale: Corticosteroids cause immunosuppression (infection risk) and hyperglycaemia, and fluid balance must be maintained; per Kenya EML/BNF steroid monitoring these are the key nursing priorities. Bone marrow suppression is a cytotoxic, not steroid, effect. 263. The common causative organism for pharyngitis is, A. Group B, beta hemolytic streptococcus B. Group A, beta hemolytic streptococcus Rationale: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is the classic bacterial cause of pharyngitis (Brunner & Suddarth; IMNCI sore throat guidance). 264. In pulmonary embolism (PE), A. There is a clot formation in the pulmonary vein and or its branches B. There is obstruction of the Pulmonary artery or one of its branches C. Trauma, pregnancy and Valsava maneuvers are common predisposing factors D. Old age, heart failure and intestinal obstruction clients are more prone Answer: B. The clot lodges in the artery, not the pulmonary vein. 265. Dumping syndrome is as a result of, A. Rapid emptying of hypertonic food from the stomach into the jejunum B. The vitamin required for normal production of RBCs is; A. calcium B. vitamin A C. folic D. vitamin K Answer: C. folic Rationale: Folic acid (folate), with vitamin B12, is required for normal red blood cell production/maturation; deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia (Kenya nutrition/haematology guidance, Brunner & Suddarth). 268. Plain insulin has peak action of; A. 8- 12hours B. 2-3 hours C. 12-16hours D. 16-30hours Answer: B. 2-3 hours Rationale: Plain/regular (short-acting soluble) insulin has onset ~30 min, peak action about 2-3 hours (Kenya EML/BNF insulin pharmacology). 269. Valsava maneuver can result to bradycardia. Which of the following activities will not stimulate valsalva’s maneuver? A. Use of stool softeners B. Enema administration C. Gaggling while tooth brushing D. Lifting heavy objects Answer: A. Use of stool softeners Rationale: Straining (enema, forceful gagging, heavy lifting) triggers the Valsalva manoeuvre; stool softeners prevent straining and therefore do NOT stimulate it (Brunner & Suddarth). The question asks which will NOT stimulate the manoeuvre. 270. What is the reason for the nurse in instructing the client to rotate the injection sites for insulin? A client has just undergone spinal fusion after experiencing herniation of a lumbar disk. The nurse would avoid which intervention to maintain client safety after this procedure? A. Use the overhead trapeze. B. Keep the head of the bed flat. C. Place pillows under the length of the legs. D. Use logrolling technique for repositioning. Answer: C. Place pillows under the length of the legs. Rationale: After spinal fusion the spine must be kept in neutral alignment; placing pillows along the full length of the legs causes spinal flexion and is avoided. Nurse Nyaruai is giving a health education talk to Mothers attending the MCH/FP clinic at Kapkoros health center. IgA Rationale: Secretory IgA is the predominant antibody passed to the infant in breast milk (especially colostrum), providing mucosal/gut protection (Kenya MCH/IMNCI, WHO breastfeeding guidance). IgG crosses the placenta, not chiefly milk. 273. Which of the following interventions would be helpful to a breastfeeding mother who is experiencing engorged breasts? A. Applying ice B. Teaching how to express her breasts in a warm shower Rationale: For a breastfeeding mother with engorgement, warmth and expression/continued feeding relieve the fullness (Myles Textbook for Midwives). Ice, bromocriptine and binders are used to suppress lactation, not for a mother who wishes to continue breastfeeding. 274. You are preparing to perform a fundal assessment on a postpartum client. Following a difficult labor and birth, a primiparous woman refuses to feed her baby four hours after delivery, she states that she is too tired and just wants to sleep. The nurse should: A. General nursing care during post-partal period includes assessment of the: A. Breasts, abdomen, and fundus B. Breasts, abdomen, and musculoskeletal system C. At the end of labor, the cervix is: A. soft and flabby B. 2cm dilated C. 1cm dilated D. a slit Answer: A. soft and flabby Rationale: At the end of labour, after full dilatation and delivery, the cervix is soft, flabby and thin; it is no longer measured in cm of dilatation (Myles Textbook for Midwives). 283. You are taking vital signs observations on a postpartum client who delivered a healthy newborn 4 hours ago. Her temperature is 100.2° F or 37.9 What is the priority nursing action? A. Increase hydration by encouraging oral fluids. B. Document the findings. C. Retake the temperature in 15 minutes D. Notify the doctor Postpartum fever is defined as a temperature of 38.7 degrees C (101.6 degrees F) or greater for the first 24 hours or greater than 38.0 degrees C (100.4 degrees F) on any two of the first 10 days postpartum. What is the best position to assess a postpartum woman’s fundus? A. On her right side. B. Semi-Fowler position. C. Supine with knees slightly flexed. D. In a chair, with feet elevated. Answer: C. The diastolic pressure is usually not affected by excitement, its increase therefore is more significant in assessment of pregnant women for pre-eclampsia. Laboratory findings that are consistent with hyperthyroidism include A. Decreased serum triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) levels B. Elevated serum thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH) levels C. Body mechanics usually prescribed for clients with low pain include:- A. Bending at knee and hips, standing straight, carrying objects close to the body. B. Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing, correct body mechanics for low-back pain prevention involve bending at the knees and hips (not the waist), keeping the back straight, and carrying objects close to the body to reduce spinal strain. 318. When a nurse is monitoring a patient for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak he/she should observe for:- A. Halo sign. B. Babinski reflex. C. Iliopsoas sign. D. Blumberg sign. Answer: A. Halo sign. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth's, CSF leak is detected by the halo (ring) sign, where drainage on gauze forms a clear ring around blood, and by glucose-positive fluid. Babinski, iliopsoas and Blumberg signs are unrelated neurological/abdominal signs. 319. The commonest cause of toxic goitre (Grave’s disease) is: - A. Pituitary tumours B. Benign thyroid C. Immunoglobulins reaction Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth's, Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSH-receptor antibodies). Iodine lack causes simple/endemic goitre, not toxic Graves' goitre. 320. Parathyroid hormone maintains fluid and electrolyte balance by A. Promoting absorption of calcium from the intestines B. Inhibiting release of calcium from the bone C. Increasing the excretion of phosphate ions by the kidneys D. Acting on the renal tubules to retain water and to decrease urinary output Answer: C. Increasing the excretion of phosphate ions by the kidneys Rationale: Parathyroid hormone raises serum calcium by mobilising calcium from bone, increasing intestinal (via vitamin D) and renal calcium reabsorption, and increasing renal excretion of phosphate. Of the options given, increasing phosphate excretion by the kidneys is the correct PTH action (Guyton/standard physiology). 321. The carcinogenic risk factors for laryngeal cancers include: A. A high-fibre diet (option C) is protective, not carcinogenic, so D is the fully correct set. 322. In Fallot’s tetralogy there is A.
