The nurse is teaching a client with myasthenia gravis about the prevention of myasthenic and cholinergic crisis. Which client activity suggests that teaching is most effective? A. Taking medications as scheduled B. Eating large, well-balanced meals C. Doing muscle-strengthening exercises D. Doing all chores early in the day while less fatigue Answer: A. Taking medications as scheduled Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, in myasthenia gravis anticholinesterase drugs must be taken exactly on schedule to maintain therapeutic levels; late/missed doses precipitate myasthenic crisis and overdose precipitates cholinergic crisis. Large meals, strenuous exercise and doing all chores early do not reliably prevent crises; adherence to the medication schedule does. 385. The client is admitted to the hospital with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which past medical history finding makes the client most at risk for this disease? A. Meningitis or encephalitis during the last 5 years B. Seizures or trauma to the brain within the last year C. Back injury or trauma to the spinal cord during the last 2 years D. Respiratory or gastrointestinal infection during the previous month Answer: D. Respiratory or gastrointestinal infection during the previous month Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, Guillain-Barre syndrome is an autoimmune polyneuropathy typically preceded (1–4 weeks prior) by a viral respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (e.g., Campylobacter). Meningitis, seizures/head trauma and spinal/back injury are not the classic antecedent risk; a recent respiratory/GI infection is. 386. A client has a neurological deficit involving the limbic system. On assessment, which finding is specific to this type of deficit? A. Is disoriented to person, place, and time B. Affect is flat, with periods of emotional lability C. Cannot recall what was eaten for breakfast today D. Demonstrates inability to add and subtract; does not know who is the president of the United States Answer: B. Affect is flat, with periods of emotional lability Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, the limbic system governs emotion and behaviour, so a deficit produces flat affect and emotional lability. Disorientation, recent-memory loss and impaired calculation/general knowledge point more to cortical/hippocampal or global cognitive dysfunction; altered emotional regulation is specific to the limbic system. 387. The nurse is evaluating the status of a client who had a craniotomy 3 days ago. Which assessment finding would indicate that the client is developing meningitis as a complication of surgery? A. A negative Kernig’s sign B. Absence of nuchal rigidity C. A positive Brudzinski’s sign D. A Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 Answer: C. A positive Brudzinski’s sign Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, meningitis produces meningeal irritation signs: nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs. A positive Brudzinski's sign indicates developing meningitis; a negative Kernig's, absent nuchal rigidity and a normal GCS of 15 would suggest NO meningitis. 388. A client with myasthenia gravis has become increasingly weaker. The health care provider prepares to identify whether the client is reacting to an overdose of the medication (cholinergic crisis) or an increasing severity of the disease (myasthenic crisis). An injection of edrophonium is administered. Which finding would indicate that the client is in a cholinergic crisis? A. No change in the condition B. Complaints of muscle spasms C. An improvement of the weakness D. A temporary worsening of the condition Answer: D. A temporary worsening of the condition Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, in the edrophonium (Tensilon) test, improvement of weakness indicates myasthenic crisis (needs more anticholinesterase), whereas temporary worsening of weakness indicates cholinergic crisis (already too much drug). Hence temporary worsening indicates cholinergic crisis. 389. The nurse is positioning the female client with increased intracranial pressure. Which of the following positions would the nurse avoid? A. Head midline B. Head turned to the side C. Neck in neutral position D. Head of bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees Answer: B. Head turned to the side Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, with increased ICP the head should be kept midline and neutral with the bed elevated 30–45 degrees to promote venous drainage; turning/rotating the head to the side obstructs jugular venous outflow and raises ICP, so it is the position to AVOID. 390. The nurse is caring for the male client who begins to experience seizure activity while in bed. Which of the following actions by the nurse would be contraindicated? A. Loosening restrictive clothing B. Restraining the client’s limbs C. Removing the pillow and raising padded side rails D. Positioning the client to side, if possible , with the head flexed forward Answer: B. Restraining the client’s limbs Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals and Brunner & Suddarth, during a seizure the nurse must NOT restrain the limbs (risks fractures/injury). Correct actions are loosening clothing, removing the pillow and padding side rails, and side-lying with head flexed forward; restraining limbs is contraindicated. 391. A female client has experienced an episode of myasthenic crisis. The nurse would assess whether the client has precipitating factors such as: A. getting too little exercise B. taking excess medication - (will cause cholinergic crisis instead) C. omitting doses of medication D. increasing intake of fatty foods Answer: C. omitting doses of medication Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, myasthenic crisis is precipitated by under-medication (omitting/missing anticholinesterase doses), infection, stress or surgery. Excess medication causes cholinergic crisis; too little exercise and fatty foods are not precipitants. Thus omitting doses precipitates myasthenic crisis. 392. A male client is having a tonic-clonic seizures. What should the nurse do first? A. Elevate the head of the bed B. Restrain the client’s arms and legs C. Place a tongue blade in the client’s mouth D. Take measures to prevent injury Answer: D. Take measures to prevent injury Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's and Brunner & Suddarth, the FIRST priority during a tonic-clonic seizure is to protect the client from injury (ease to the floor/side-lying, clear the area, cushion the head). Do not restrain limbs or insert a tongue blade; elevating the head is not the priority. Injury prevention/safety comes first. 393. The nurse is teaching the female client with myasthenia gravis about the prevention of myasthenic and cholinergic crises. The nurse tells the client that this is most effectively done by: A. Eating large, well-balanced meals B. Doing muscle -strengthening exercises C. Doing all chores early in the day while less fatigued D. Taking medications on time to maintain therapeutic blood levels Answer: D. Taking medications on time to maintain therapeutic blood levels Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, prevention of both myasthenic and cholinergic crises depends on taking anticholinesterase medication precisely on time to keep therapeutic blood levels. Large meals, muscle-strengthening exercise and doing all chores early are not effective preventive measures. 394. Which of the following neurotransmitters is known to be associated with sleep, mood and appetite? A. Acetylcholine B. Dopamine C. Serotonin D. GABA Answer: C. Serotonin Rationale: Per standard physiology (Brunner & Suddarth / Lewis) and psychiatric nursing texts, serotonin (5-HT) regulates sleep, mood and appetite. Acetylcholine (muscle/memory), dopamine (movement/reward) and GABA (inhibition) do not fit this triad; serotonin does. 395. The neurons of the motor pathway control: A. Stress reaction B. Organs and glands C. Involuntary muscles D. Voluntary muscles Answer: D. Voluntary muscles Rationale: Per anatomy & physiology texts, the motor (somatic) pathway carries efferent impulses controlling voluntary (skeletal) muscles. Involuntary muscles, organs and glands are controlled by the autonomic nervous system; hence voluntary muscles is correct. 396. The area of the brain which is involved in the understanding of meaning is: A. Broca’s area B. association areas C. Wernicke area D. Motor speech area Answer: C. Wernicke area Rationale: Per neuroanatomy (Brunner & Suddarth), Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal lobe) is responsible for comprehension/understanding of language meaning. Broca's/motor speech area handles speech production; general association areas integrate information, but understanding of meaning is specifically Wernicke's area. 397. Parkinson’s disease , is caused by the degeneration of neurons in an area of the brain called the: A. Substantia nigra B. Basal ganglia C. Cerebellum D. Corpus callosum Answer: A. Substantia nigra Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, reducing dopamine. Although the basal ganglia circuit is affected, the primary site of neuronal degeneration is the substantia nigra. 398. The division of the nervous system which controls the involuntary muscles, organs, and glands is: A. Somatic nervous system B. Autonomic nervous system C. Central nervous system D. The motor pathway of the CNS Answer: B. Autonomic nervous system Rationale: Per anatomy & physiology texts, the autonomic nervous system controls involuntary muscles, organs and glands (via sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions). The somatic system controls voluntary muscle; the CNS is the integrating centre. Hence autonomic nervous system is correct. 399. A client is unconscious following a tonic-clonic seizure. What should the nurse do FIRST? A. Place the client in a side-lying position B. Check the pulse C. Administer Valium D. Place a tongue blade in the mouth (Never do this! Places client in danger!) Answer: A. Place the client in a side-lying position Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's and Brunner & Suddarth, in the postictal unconscious client the FIRST action is to place them in a side-lying (recovery) position to maintain a patent airway and prevent aspiration. Never insert a tongue blade; pulse check and Valium are not the immediate priority over airway positioning. 400. The nurse enters the room as the client is beginning to have a tonic-clonic seizure. What action should the nurse implement first? A. Determine if the client is incontinent of urine or stool. B. Provide the client with privacy during the seizure. C. Note the first thing the client does in the seizure. D. Assess the size of the client’s pupils. Answer: C. Note the first thing the client does in the seizure. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, once safety is ensured the nurse's key nursing action at seizure onset is accurate observation/documentation, beginning with noting the first thing the client does (onset/aura and initial movements), which aids diagnosis and localization. Checking incontinence, providing privacy and pupil size are secondary to observing the seizure's onset. ⚠ More than one defensible answer 401. The nurse is teaching a class on the prevention of cerebrovascular accidents. Which of the following risk factors should the nurse identify as the most important factor contributing to a stroke? A. Sedentary lifestyle B. Smoking C. Obesity D. Hypertension Answer: D. Hypertension Rationale: Per Kenya MOH NCD guidelines and Brunner & Suddarth, hypertension is the single most important MODIFIABLE risk factor for stroke (cerebrovascular accident). Smoking, obesity and sedentary lifestyle also contribute, but hypertension is the leading contributing factor. 402. The nurse is assessing a 37-year-old client diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Which of the following symptoms would the nurse expect to find? A. Flaccid muscles B. Tremors at rest C. Absent deep tendon reflexes D. Vision changes Answer: D. Vision changes Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, multiple sclerosis classically presents with visual disturbances (optic neuritis, diplopia, blurred vision), along with spasticity, hyperreflexia and intention (not resting) tremor. Flaccid muscles, resting tremor and absent deep tendon reflexes are not typical of MS; vision changes are the expected finding. 403. If a male client experienced a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) that damaged the hypothalamus, the nurse would anticipate that the client has problems with: A. Thinking and reasoning B. Body temperature control C. Balance and equilibrium D. Visual acuity Answer: B. Body temperature control Rationale: The hypothalamus is the principal thermoregulatory centre (also controlling hunger, thirst, and neuroendocrine function). Damage impairs body temperature control. Thinking/reasoning is cortical (frontal), balance is cerebellar, and visual acuity is occipital/optic pathway (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 404. During recovery from a cerebrovascular accident (CVA), a female client is given nothing by mouth, to help prevent aspiration. To determine when the client is ready for a liquid diet, the nurse assesses the client’s swallowing ability once each shift. This assessment evaluates A. Cranial nerves III and V B. Cranial nerves IX and X C. Cranial nerves I and II D. Cranial nerves VI and VIII Answer: B. Cranial nerves IX and X Rationale: Swallowing (gag reflex) is mediated by the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves. Assessing swallowing ability tests these cranial nerves before advancing diet post-CVA (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 405. A male client is admitted with a cervical spine injury sustained during a diving accident. When planning this client’s care, the nurse should assign highest priority to which nursing diagnosis? A. Disturbed sensory perception (tactile) B. Self-care deficit: dressing /grooming C. Impaired physical mobility D. Ineffective breathing pattern Answer: D. Ineffective breathing pattern Rationale: A cervical (high) spinal cord injury threatens the diaphragm and respiratory muscles (C3-C5 innervate the diaphragm). Airway/breathing is the highest priority per ABC prioritisation; the other diagnoses are important but not immediately life-threatening (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 406. Demyelination is defined as; A. Loss of an axon in a neuron B. Loss of dendrites in a neuron C. Loss of protective sheath surrounding neurons D. Loss of connective tissue between neurons Answer: C. Loss of protective sheath surrounding neurons Rationale: Demyelination is the loss/destruction of the myelin sheath surrounding nerve fibres (as in multiple sclerosis), slowing nerve conduction (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 407. Failure of muscle coordination , including unsteady movements and staggering walk, due to disorders in the cerebellum is called? A. Anoxia B. Dyslexia C. Paraplegia D. Ataxia Answer: D. Ataxia Rationale: Ataxia is impaired muscle coordination causing unsteady, staggering gait, characteristically due to cerebellar dysfunction. Anoxia is oxygen lack, dyslexia is a reading disorder, and paraplegia is lower-limb paralysis (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 408. Which part of the brain regulates heartbeat, breathing and other vital functions? A. Grey matter B. Brain stem C. Occipital lobe D. White matter Answer: B. Brain stem Rationale: The brain stem (specifically the medulla oblongata) contains the cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centres regulating heartbeat, breathing and other vital functions (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 409. Common complications of spinal cord injury include each of the following EXCEPT? A. Pressure sores B. Deep vein thrombosis C. Diarrhoea D. Urinary Tract infections Answer: C. Diarrhoea Rationale: Spinal cord injury commonly causes pressure sores, DVT (from immobility), and UTIs (from neurogenic bladder/catheterisation). Constipation, not diarrhoea, results from neurogenic bowel; thus diarrhoea is the exception (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 410. Broca’s area is located in the A. Brain stem B. Frontal lobe C. Parietal lobe D. Temporal lobe Answer: B. Frontal lobe Rationale: Broca's area (motor speech centre) lies in the inferior frontal lobe of the dominant hemisphere; damage causes expressive (non-fluent) aphasia (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 411. Wernicke area is located in the A. Brain stem B. Parietal lobe C. Temporal lobe D. Frontal lobe Answer: C. Temporal lobe Rationale: Wernicke's area (receptive/sensory speech centre) is located in the posterior superior temporal lobe of the dominant hemisphere; damage causes receptive (fluent) aphasia (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 412. The presence of ptosis suggests damage to cranial nerve: A. IV B. V C. III D. VII Answer: C. III Rationale: The oculomotor nerve (III) supplies the levator palpebrae superioris, which elevates the upper eyelid; its damage causes ptosis (drooping eyelid) along with a 'down and out' eye (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). 413. A 60-year-old man complains of extremely severe, sharp, shooting pain in his face. Hee describes the episodes as being “like a bolt of electricity”that is brought about by touching a specific area. Lasta about 60 seconds, and occur many times during the day. Neurologic examination is completely normal but it is noted that part of his face is unshaven because he fears to touch that area. Aspirin/NSAIDs and vasoconstrictors are ineffective (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing; Kenya EML). 414. Which of the following function is controlled by parasympathetic system? A. Pupil constriction B. Acceleration of heart beat C. Stimulation of sweat glands D. Contraction of hair muscles Answer: A. Pupil constriction Rationale: Parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) stimulation causes pupil constriction (miosis), slows the heart, and reduces secretions. Acceleration of heart rate, sweating, and pilo-erection are sympathetic responses (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals; Brunner & Suddarth's). 415. Which one of the following is NOT a probable sign of the second stage of labour? A. uterine contractions B. No cervix felt on vaginal examination C. Rupture of membranes D. Rupture of membranes can occur at any stage and is not a specific sign of second stage, so it is the exception (Myles Textbook for Midwives). 416. You are caring for a woman in the second stage of labor. The client is experiencing uterine contractions every 2 minutes and cries out in pain with each contraction. Fear of losing control Rationale: Crying out in pain with each contraction during transition reflects fear of losing control, a recognised psychological response requiring reassurance and support. It is not exhaustion, involuntary grunting (an urge to push), or Valsalva (Myles Textbook for Midwives). ⚠ More than one defensible answer 417. In which one of the following stages is the placenta delivered? A. Stage 1, latent phase B. Stage 1, active phase C. Stage2 D. Stage 3 Answer: D. Endogenous oxytocin is released from the: A. anterior pituitary gland B. cervix C. posterior pituitary gland D. uterus Answer: C. posterior pituitary gland Rationale: Oxytocin is synthesised in the hypothalamus and released (stored) from the posterior pituitary gland; it stimulates uterine contraction and milk ejection (Myles Textbook for Midwives; physiology texts). 423. The midwife is caring for a woman in labour. She determines that the woman is beginning the 2nd stage of labour when which of the following signs is noted? A. Regular contractions and ruptured membranes are not defining signs (Myles Textbook for Midwives). 424. Which of the following is true about congenital abnormalities? A. When resuscitating a neonate who has neonatal asphyxia after how long should the midwife use ambubag A. After 30 seconds of oxygen by face mask B. Which of the following is the most appropriate feature seen in symmetric growth retarded infant? A. Weight is depressed more than length or head circumference. B. A new born infant was delivered in your maternity unit an hour ago. The skin of this infant appears to be red, wrinkly with ribs visible under the skin. When was the infant probably born? A. Which statement is true about meconium? A. Meconium is 1st found in the foetal ileum between the 20th and 26th weeks of gestation B. Which of the following is true about twin to twin transfusion syndrome? A. The smaller twin has the greatest risk of cardiac compromise B. The larger twin is often stuck to the uterine wall C. What is the greatest risk of retained products of conception in the immediate post partum period? A. Uterine atony B. Uterine inversion C. Uterine rupture D. Uterine tenderness Answer: A. Encourage the patient to increase his fluid intake Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals, after a barium enema fluids and often a mild laxative are given to promote elimination of retained barium and prevent constipation/impaction. Barium is inert and not radioactive (B). 498. Passive range of motion exercises; A. Are performed to prevent nosocomial infections. B. Helps to prevent joints rigidity and contractures. C. Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals, passive ROM exercises maintain joint mobility and prevent stiffness and contractures in patients unable to move independently. They do not prevent infections (A). 499. The Korotkoff sounds heard while measuring blood pressure present in the order of, A. Tapping, Swishing, Knocking, muffling and silence B. Swishing, Tapping, Silence, muffling and knocking C. Knocking, Tapping, Swishing, muffling, silence D. Silence, Tapping, Knocking, Swishing and Muffling B A Answer: A. Tapping, Swishing, Knocking, muffling and silence Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's, the five Korotkoff phases occur in order: sharp tapping (Phase I, systolic), swishing/murmur (Phase II), knocking (Phase III), muffling (Phase IV), then silence/disappearance (Phase V, diastolic). 500. In sickle cell anaemia patients, A. The structure of haemoglobin molecule is not affected. B. Prophylactic administration of folic acid and pneumococcal vaccine is recommended C. Prophylactic administration of folic acid and pneumococcal vaccine is recommended Rationale: Per Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols and Brunner & Suddarth, sickle cell patients require daily folic acid (increased erythropoiesis) and pneumococcal prophylaxis/vaccination due to functional asplenia. The Hb structure IS abnormal (A false); routine immediate transfusion in every crisis is not encouraged (C). 501. Hyperkalemia commonly occurs in the following, A. Burns, pneumonia and congestive cardiac failure. B. Renal failure, crush injuries and burns. C. Digitalis toxicity, DKA and hyperthyroidism. D. Overuse of potassium sparing diuretics, CCF and liver cirrhosis C B Answer: B. Renal failure, crush injuries and burns. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, hyperkalemia results from impaired renal excretion (renal failure) and massive cellular potassium release in crush injuries and burns. DKA typically shows shifting but hyperthyroidism is not a classic cause (C). 502. The route that achieves the quickest absorption and effects of a drug is the, A. Subcutaneous B. Intradermal C. Intramuscular D. Oral D C Answer: C. Intramuscular Rationale: Among the given parenteral/enteral routes, intramuscular injection has the richest vascular bed, giving faster absorption than subcutaneous, intradermal, or oral. Per Brunner & Suddarth pharmacology, IM absorption is quickest of these options (IV not listed). 503. In simple mastectomy:- A. Pectoralis major muscle and the entire breast is excised B. Removing axillary nodes (D) describes modified radical mastectomy. 504. Reed Sternberg cell is a pathologic hallmark essential in diagnosis of:- A. Hodgkin’s disease B. Acute myeloid leukemia C. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia D. Non-hodgkin disease Answer: A. Hodgkin’s disease Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, the Reed-Sternberg cell is the pathognomonic hallmark used to diagnose Hodgkin's lymphoma. It is absent in non-Hodgkin lymphoma and the leukemias. 505. Characteristics of 1st degree burns include:- A. Erythema and pain B. Chilling and dry wounds C. Healing by scaling, painless wounds D. Erythema and pain Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, first-degree (superficial) burns involve only the epidermis and present with erythema, pain, and no blistering (e.g., sunburn). Painless black/leathery wounds (D) indicate full-thickness burns. 506. In rheumatoid arthritis, inflammation of the jounts begins in the:- A. Hip, ankle,elbow B. Feet, wrist, toes C. Shoulder, fingers, wrist D. Clavicle, hands, fingers D C Answer: B. Feet, wrist, toes Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, rheumatoid arthritis typically begins symmetrically in the small joints of the hands and feet—wrists, MCP/PIP joints, and toes—before affecting larger joints. 507. The main aim of escharotomy in treatment of full thickness burns is to:- A. Improve oxygenation of the burnt tissues B. Remove the dead tissues C. Allow underlying viable tissues to expand D. Allow underlying viable tissues to expand Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, escharotomy incises the constricting inelastic eschar of circumferential full-thickness burns to relieve pressure, allowing underlying tissue to expand and restoring circulation/ventilation. 508. Low—not high—estrogen and adequate vitamin D/sun are protective, making A and B incorrect. 509. Rhesus factor is found in the cell membrane of the:- A. Lymphocytes B. Granulocytes C. Erythrocytes D. Plaques obstruct the artery Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, atherosclerosis is the accumulation of lipid plaques within the coronary arteries, narrowing the lumen and impeding arterial blood flow to the myocardium. 511. The hypogastric region of the abdominopelvic cavity is; A. Inferior to the umbilical region, medial to the right iliac region B. Lateral to the left iliac region, superior to the umbilical region C. The most appropriate nursing action when a client begins to cough and has difficulty breathing during nasogastric tube insertion is; A. Inserting the tube quickly B. Pulling the tube back a little and wait until the respiratory distress subsides D D Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's, coughing and dyspnea during NG insertion suggest the tube has entered the airway; the nurse should withdraw the tube slightly and pause until distress resolves before advancing again. Rationale: Per Kozier & Erb's, expected outcomes for impaired gas exchange are measurable normal respiratory function: respiratory rate <20/min and normal (pink) skin colour indicating adequate oxygenation. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, lumbar puncture is performed below the spinal cord's end (L1-L2), typically in the L3-L4 (or L4-L5) interspace to avoid cord injury. Thoracic sites (A, B) are unsafe. 516. In chronic bronchitis;- A. There is cough and sputum production for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. B. Astigmatism is refractive error, presbyopia is age-related near-vision loss, and amblyopia is 'lazy eye'. 518. When assessing a client with possible Cushing’s syndrome you would expect to find; A. While hemorrhage and hypocalcemia are risks, airway patency takes priority. 523. immediately after esophageal surgery the priority nursing assessment concerns the client's A. incision B. respiration C. level of pain D. nasogastric tube Answer: B. respiration Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, following esophageal surgery (thoracic approach) the priority assessment is respiratory status/airway and breathing, as the surgery affects the chest and diaphragm and impairs ventilation. The 6-month-old client with a ventral septal defect is receiving Digitalis for regulation of his heart rate. Which finding should be reported to the doctor? A. Blood pressure of 126/80 B. A client with vaginal cancer is being treated with a radioactive vaginal implant. The client’s husband asks the nurse if he can spend the night with his wife. The nurse should explain that: A. The nurse is caring for a client hospitalized with a facial stroke. Which diet selection would be suited to the client? A. Roast beef sandwich, potato chips, pickle spear, iced tea B. The physician has prescribed Nexium (esomeprazole) for a client with erosive gastritis. The nurse should administer the medication: A. 30 minutes before meals B. With each meal C. When the nurse checks the fundus of a client on the first postpartum day, she notes that the fundus is firm, is at the level of the umbilicus, and is displaced to the right. The nurse working the organ transplant unit is caring for a client with a white blood cell count of 450. During evening visitation, a visitor brings a basket of fruit. What action should the nurse take? A. Allow the client to keep the fruit B. Place the fruit next to the bed for easy access by the client C. Offer to wash the fruit for the client D. Tell the family members to take the fruit home Answer: D. Tell the family members to take the fruit home Rationale: A WBC of 450 indicates severe neutropenia; fresh fruit harbours bacteria/fungi and is contraindicated in neutropenic precautions, so it should be removed (Brunner & Suddarth's, neutropenic care / IPC principles). 556. The client admitted 2 days earlier that a lung resection accidentally pulls out the chest tube. Which action by the nurse indicates understanding of the management of chest tubes? A. Order a chest x-ray B. Reinsert the tube C. Cover the insertion site with a Vaseline gauze D. Call the doctor Answer: C. Cover the insertion site with a Vaseline gauze Rationale: An accidentally dislodged chest tube requires immediate application of an occlusive (Vaseline) dressing to prevent air entry and tension pneumothorax, then notify the physician (Brunner & Suddarth's, chest drainage management). 557. A client being treated with sodium warfarin has a Protime of 120 seconds. Which intervention would be most important to include in the nursing care plan? A. Assess for signs of abnormal bleeding B. Anticipate an increase in the Coumadin dosage C. Instruct the client regarding the drug therapy D. Increase the frequency of neurological assessments Answer: A. Assess for signs of abnormal bleeding Rationale: A Protime of 120 seconds is grossly prolonged, indicating warfarin over-anticoagulation and high bleeding risk; the priority is to assess for abnormal bleeding (Brunner & Suddarth's / Kenya EML anticoagulant monitoring). 558. Which selection would provide the most calcium for the client who is 4 months pregnant? A. A granola bar B. A bran muffin C. A cup of yogurt D. A glass of fruit juice Answer: C. A cup of yogurt Rationale: Yogurt is a dairy product and the richest calcium source among the options, important for the increased calcium demand in pregnancy (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals; Kenya maternal nutrition guidelines). 559. A 6-year-old client is admitted to the unit with a hemoglobin of 6g/dL. The physician has written an order to transfuse 2 units of whole blood. When discussing the treatment, the child’s mother tells the nurse that she does not believe in having blood transfusions and that she will not allow her child to have the treatment. What nursing action is most appropriate? A. Ask the mother to leave while the blood transfusion is in progress B. Encourage the mother to reconsider C. Explain the consequences without treatment D. Notify the physician of the mother’s refusal Answer: D. Notify the physician of the mother’s refusal Rationale: When a parent refuses treatment for a minor, the nurse cannot coerce or force treatment; the appropriate action is to notify the physician so legal/ethical processes can follow (Professional ethics & law; Kozier & Erb's on informed consent/refusal). 560. The nurse is evaluating nutritional outcomes for a with anorexia nervosa. Which data best indicates that the plan of care is effective? A. The client selects a balanced diet from the menu. B. The client’s hemoglobin and hematocrit improve. C. The client’s tissue turgor improves. D. The client gains weight. Answer: D. The client gains weight. Rationale: In anorexia nervosa the primary nutritional goal is restoration of body weight; weight gain is the best objective indicator that the nutritional plan is effective (Brunner & Suddarth's / mental health nursing). 561. A 43-year-old African American male is admitted with sickle cell anemia. The nurse plans to assess circulation in the lower extremities every 2 hours. Which of the following outcome criteria would the nurse use? A. Body temperature of 37.2 celsius or less B. Toes moved in active range of motion C. Sensation reported when soles of feet are touched D. Capillary refill of < 3 seconds Answer: D. Capillary refill of < 3 seconds Rationale: In sickle cell anemia, monitoring peripheral circulation is best evaluated by capillary refill; a refill under 3 seconds is the outcome criterion indicating adequate lower-extremity perfusion (Brunner & Suddarth's, haematologic disorders). 562. A 30-year-old male from Haiti is brought to the emergency department in sickle cell crisis. What is the best position for this client? A. Side-lying with knees flexed B. Knee-chest C. High Fowler's with knees flexed D. Semi-Fowler's with legs extended on the bed Answer: D. Semi-Fowler's with legs extended on the bed Rationale: In sickle cell crisis, positions that flex joints and impede circulation are avoided; semi-Fowler's with legs extended promotes comfort, oxygenation and unrestricted circulation (Brunner & Suddarth's, sickle cell crisis management). 563. A 25-year-old male is admitted in sickle cell crisis. Which of the following interventions would be of highest priority for this client? A. Taking hourly blood pressures with mechanical cuff B. Encouraging fluid intake of at least 200mL per hour C. Position in high Fowler's with knee gatch raised D. Administering Tylenol as ordered Answer: B. Encouraging fluid intake of at least 200mL per hour Rationale: Hydration is the highest priority in sickle cell crisis because it reduces blood viscosity, promotes circulation and limits further sickling and vaso-occlusion (Brunner & Suddarth's, sickle cell crisis). 564. Which of the following foods would the nurse encourage the client in sickle cell crisis to eat? A. Peaches B. Cottage cheese C. Popsicle D. Lima beans Answer: C. Popsicle Rationale: Fluid intake is essential in sickle cell crisis; a popsicle provides additional fluids to support hydration and reduce sickling, making it the best choice to encourage (Brunner & Suddarth's, sickle cell crisis hydration). 565. A newly admitted client has sickle cell crisis. The nurse is planning care based on assessment of the client. The client is complaining of severe pain in his feet and hands. The pulse oximetry is 92. Which of the following interventions would be implemented first? Assume that there are orders for each intervention. A. Adjust the room temperature B. Give a bolus of IV fluids C. Start O2 D. Administer meperidine (Demerol) 75mg IV push Answer: C. Start O2 Rationale: With a pulse oximetry of 92 and vaso-occlusive pain, correcting hypoxia by starting oxygen is implemented first to reduce further sickling, following the ABC priority (Brunner & Suddarth's, sickle cell crisis oxygenation). 566. The nurse is instructing a client with iron-deficiency anemia. Which of the following meal plans would the nurse expect the client to select? A. Roast beef, gelatin salad, green beans, and peach pie B. Chicken salad sandwich, coleslaw, French fries, ice cream C. Egg salad on wheat bread, carrot sticks, lettuce salad, raisin pie D. Pork chop, creamed potatoes, corn, and coconut cake Answer: C. Egg salad on wheat bread, carrot sticks, lettuce salad, raisin pie Rationale: Iron-rich choices include eggs, whole wheat, leafy green vegetables and raisins (dried fruit); this meal provides the most dietary iron for iron-deficiency anemia (Kenya nutrition guidelines; Brunner & Suddarth's). 567. Clients with sickle cell anemia are taught to avoid activities that cause hypoxia and hypoxemia. Which of the following activities would the nurse recommend? A. A bus trip to the Museum of Natural History Rationale: Activities causing hypoxia (high altitude in the Rocky Mountains, cold snow-skiing, unpressurised/altitude air travel) must be avoided; a low-altitude bus trip is safe (Brunner & Suddarth's, sickle cell patient education). 568. The nurse is conducting an admission assessment of a client with vitamin B12 deficiency. Which of the following would the nurse include in the physical assessment? A. Palpate the spleen B. Take the blood pressure C. Examine the feet for petechiae D. Examine the tongue Answer: D. Examine the tongue Rationale: Vitamin B12 deficiency characteristically causes glossitis (a smooth, beefy-red, sore tongue); examining the tongue is the relevant physical assessment finding (Brunner & Suddarth's, megaloblastic/pernicious anemia). 569. An African American female comes to the outpatient clinic. The physician suspects vitamin B12 deficiency anemia. Shins Answer: C. Roof of the mouth Rationale: In dark-skinned clients jaundice is best detected in the hard palate (roof of the mouth) and sclera where the yellow discoloration is most visible (Kozier & Erb's, assessment of skin colour in dark-skinned clients). 570. The nurse is conducting a physical assessment on a client with anemia. Which of the following clinical manifestations would be most indicative of the anemia? A. BP 146/88 B. Respirations 28 shallow C. Weight gain of 10 pounds in 6 months D. Pink complexion Answer: B. Respirations 28 shallow Rationale: Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity, causing compensatory tachypnea and dyspnea; increased shallow respirations (28) is the most indicative manifestation, while pink complexion would be inconsistent with anemia (Brunner & Suddarth's, anemia assessment). 571. A 33-year-old male is being evaluated for possible acute leukemia. Which of the following would the nurse inquire about as a part of the assessment? A. The client collects stamps as a hobby. B. The client recently lost his job as a postal worker. C. The client had radiation for treatment of Hodgkin's disease as a teenager. D. The client's brother had leukemia as a child. Answer: C. The client had radiation for treatment of Hodgkin's disease as a teenager. Rationale: Prior radiation therapy is a well-established risk factor for developing acute leukemia; this history is the relevant assessment inquiry (Brunner & Suddarth's, leukemia risk factors). 572. An African American client is admitted with acute leukemia. The nurse is assessing for signs and symptoms of bleeding. Where is the best site for examining for the presence of petechiae? A. The abdomen B. The thorax C. The earlobes D. The soles of the feet Answer: C. The earlobes Rationale: In dark-skinned clients petechiae are best assessed in areas of lighter pigmentation with thin skin such as the earlobes and oral mucosa/conjunctiva (Kozier & Erb's, skin assessment in dark-skinned clients). 573. Which of the following would be the priority nursing diagnosis for the adult client with acute leukemia? A. Oral mucous membrane, altered related to chemotherapy B. Risk for injury related to thrombocytopenia C. Fatigue related to the disease process D. Interrupted family processes related to life-threatening illness of a family member Answer: B. Risk for injury related to thrombocytopenia Rationale: In acute leukemia, thrombocytopenia predisposes to life-threatening hemorrhage; risk for injury/bleeding is the priority (physiologic safety) nursing diagnosis (Brunner & Suddarth's, leukemia nursing care). 574. A 21-year-old male with Hodgkin's lymphoma is a senior at the local university. He is engaged to be married and is to begin a new job upon graduation. The home health nurse is visiting a client with autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura (ATP). Conservation of energy Answer: A. A client with a pituitary tumor has had a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy. Which of the following interventions would be appropriate for this client? A. Elevate the head of the bed 30° Rationale: After transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, the head of the bed is elevated 30° to reduce pressure on the sella and CSF leak risk; coughing, Valsalva and Trendelenburg increase intracranial pressure and are contraindicated (Brunner & Suddarth's, hypophysectomy care). 577. The client with a history of diabetes insipidus is admitted with polyuria, polydipsia, and mental confusion. The priority intervention for this client is: A. Measure the urinary output B. Check the vital signs C. Encourage increased fluid intake D. Weigh the client Answer: B. Check the vital signs Rationale: Diabetes insipidus with polyuria and confusion risks severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock; assessing vital signs is the priority to detect fluid volume/hemodynamic instability (Brunner & Suddarth's, diabetes insipidus). 578. A client with hemophilia has a nosebleed. Which nursing action is most appropriate to control the bleeding? A. Place the client in a sitting position with the head hyperextended B. Apply ice packs to the forehead and back of the neck Answer: C. Pinch the soft lower part of the nose for a minimum of 5 minutes Rationale: For epistaxis in hemophilia, applying steady pressure by pinching the soft lower nose (with the client upright, head forward) controls bleeding; hyperextension and tight packing are avoided (Basic nursing/first aid; Brunner & Suddarth's, hemophilia). 579. A client has had a unilateral adrenalectomy to remove a tumor. To prevent complications, the most important measurement in the immediate postoperative period for the nurse to take is: A. Blood pressure B. Temperature C. Output D. Specific gravity Answer: A. Blood pressure Rationale: After adrenalectomy, adrenal hormone fluctuations cause hemodynamic instability (hypotension or hypertension); blood pressure is the most important immediate postoperative measurement (Brunner & Suddarth's, adrenal surgery). 580. A client with Addison's disease has been admitted with a history of nausea and vomiting for the past 3 days. The client is receiving IV glucocorticoids (Solu-Medrol). Sodium and potassium levels monitored Rationale: In Addison's disease/adrenal insufficiency the key electrolyte disturbance is hyponatremia and hyperkalemia; monitoring sodium and potassium is the priority intervention (Brunner & Suddarth's, Addisonian crisis). 581. A client had a total thyroidectomy yesterday. The client is complaining of tingling around the mouth and in the fingers and toes. What would the nurses' next action be? A. Obtain a crash cart B. Check the calcium level C. Assess the dressing for drainage D. Assess the blood pressure for hypertension Answer: B. Check the calcium level Rationale: Tingling of the mouth, fingers and toes after thyroidectomy signals hypocalcemia from accidental parathyroid injury; the nurse should check the calcium level and watch for tetany (Brunner & Suddarth's, post-thyroidectomy complications). 582. A 32-year-old mother of three is brought to the clinic. Her pulse is 52, there is a weight gain of 30 pounds in 4 months, and the client is wearing two sweaters. The client is diagnosed with hypothyroidism. Which of the following nursing diagnoses is of highest priority? A. Impaired physical mobility related to decreased endurance B. Hypothermia r/t decreased metabolic rate C. Disturbed thought processes r/t interstitial edema D. Decreased cardiac output r/t bradycardia Answer: D. Decreased cardiac output r/t bradycardia Rationale: Using the airway/circulation priority, the pulse of 52 (bradycardia) makes decreased cardiac output the highest-priority (physiologic) diagnosis in hypothyroidism (Brunner & Suddarth's, hypothyroidism; Maslow/ABC prioritisation). 583. A primigravida, age 42, is 6 weeks pregnant. Based on the client's age, her infant is at risk for: A. Down syndrome B. Respiratory distress syndrome C. Turner's syndrome D. Pathological jaundice Answer: A. Down syndrome Rationale: Advanced maternal age (42) markedly increases the risk of chromosomal trisomies, most notably Down syndrome (trisomy 21) (Myles Textbook for Midwives; Kenya maternal care guidelines). 584. A client with a missed abortion at 29 weeks gestation is admitted to the hospital. The client will most likely be treated with: A. Magnesium sulfate B. Calcium gluconate C. Dinoprostone (Prostin E.) D. Bromocriptine (Pardel) Answer: C. Dinoprostone (Prostin E.) Rationale: A missed abortion at 29 weeks requires evacuation; dinoprostone (a prostaglandin E) is used to induce cervical ripening and uterine contractions to expel the retained products (Myles Textbook for Midwives; Kenya maternal guidelines on induction). 585. A client with preeclampsia has been receiving an infusion containing magnesium sulfate for a blood pressure that is 160/80; deep tendon reflexes are 1 plus, and the urinary output for the past hour is 100mL. The nurse should: A. Continue the infusion of magnesium sulfate while monitoring the client's blood pressure B. Stop the infusion of magnesium sulfate and contact the physician C. Slow the infusion rate and turn the client on her left side D. Administer calcium gluconate IV push and continue to monitor the blood pressure Answer: A. Continue the infusion of magnesium sulfate while monitoring the client's blood pressure Rationale: Per Kenya National Maternal guidelines/Myles, MgSO4 is withheld only for magnesium toxicity signs: respiratory depression, absent reflexes, or urine output <30mL/hr (<100mL/4hr). Here reflexes are present (1+) and output is adequate (100mL/hr), so the infusion is safely continued with monitoring. 586. Which statement made by the nurse describes the inheritance pattern of autosomal recessive disorders? A. An affected newborn has unaffected parents. B. An affected newborn has one affected parent. C. Affected parents have a one in four chance of passing on the defective gene. D. Affected parents have unaffected children who are carriers. Answer: A. An affected newborn has unaffected parents. Rationale: Per genetics (Brunner & Suddarth), in autosomal recessive inheritance both unaffected parents are typically heterozygous carriers, so an affected child is born to phenotypically unaffected parents. The 1-in-4 risk refers to two carrier (not affected) parents, making that option imprecise. 587. A pregnant client, age 32, asks the nurse why her doctor has recommended a serum alpha fetoprotein. The nurse should explain that the doctor has recommended the test: A. Because it is a state law B. To detect cardiovascular defects C. Because of her age D. To detect neurological defects Answer: D. To detect neurological defects Rationale: Per Myles/antenatal screening, maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein screens for neural tube (neurological) defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly; elevated AFP indicates open NTDs. Age relates to Down screening, not AFP alone. 588. A client with hypothyroidism asks the nurse if she will still need to take thyroid medication during the pregnancy. The nurse's response is based on the knowledge that: A. There is no need to take thyroid medication because the fetus's thyroid produces a thyroid-stimulating hormone. B. Regulation of thyroid medication is more difficult because the thyroid gland increases in size during pregnancy. C. It is more difficult to maintain thyroid regulation during pregnancy due to a slowing of metabolism. D. Fetal growth is arrested if thyroid medication is continued during pregnancy. Answer: B. Regulation of thyroid medication is more difficult because the thyroid gland increases in size during pregnancy. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth/maternal endocrine physiology, thyroid demand and gland size increase in pregnancy so thyroid replacement often needs upward adjustment; medication must be continued, not stopped. Metabolism rises (not slows) in pregnancy. 589. The nurse is responsible for performing a neonatal assessment on a full-term infant. At 1 minute, the nurse would expect to find: A. An apical pulse of 100 B. An absence of tonus C. Cyanosis of the feet and hands D. Jaundice of the skin and sclera Answer: C. Cyanosis of the feet and hands Rationale: Per Basic Paediatric Protocols/newborn assessment, acrocyanosis (bluish hands and feet) is a normal finding at 1 minute due to peripheral circulation. Apical pulse should be 120-160, and jaundice at 1 minute is abnormal. 590. A client with sickle cell anemia is admitted to the labor and delivery unit during the first phase of labor. The nurse should anticipate the client's need for: A. Supplemental oxygen B. Fluid restriction C. Blood transfusion D. Delivery by Caesarean section Answer: A. Supplemental oxygen Rationale: Per Kenya haematology/maternal guidelines, in sickle cell disease during labor the priority is preventing hypoxia and sickling crisis, so supplemental oxygen and hydration are anticipated. Fluid restriction is contraindicated as it promotes sickling. 591. A client with diabetes has an order for ultrasonography. Preparation for an ultrasound includes: A. Increasing fluid intake B. Limiting ambulation C. Administering an enema D. Withholding food for 8 hours Answer: A. Increasing fluid intake Rationale: Per obstetric ultrasound preparation (Myles), a full bladder from increased fluid intake elevates the uterus and provides an acoustic window for imaging in pregnancy. Withholding food and enemas are not required for obstetric/abdominal ultrasound. 592. An infant who weighs 8 pounds at birth would be expected to weigh how many pounds at 1 year? A. 14 pounds B. 16 pounds C. 18 pounds D. 24 pounds Answer: D. 24 pounds Rationale: Per Basic Paediatric Protocols/growth norms, an infant's birth weight roughly triples by 1 year; 8 pounds x 3 = 24 pounds. Doubling occurs by ~5-6 months. 593. A pregnant client with a history of alcohol addiction is scheduled for a nonstress test. The nonstress test: A. Determines the lung maturity of the fetus B. Measures the activity of the fetus C. Shows the effect of contractions on the fetal heart rate D. Measures the neurological well-being of the fetus Answer: B. Measures the activity of the fetus Rationale: Per Myles antenatal testing, a nonstress test evaluates fetal heart rate accelerations in response to fetal movement (activity), reflecting well-being. Contraction effects are assessed by the contraction stress test, and lung maturity by L/S ratio. 594. A full-term male has hypospadias. Which statement describes hypospadias? A. The urethra opens on the ventral side of the penis. Rationale: Per Basic Paediatric Protocols/paediatric surgery, hypospadias is a congenital anomaly in which the urethral meatus opens on the ventral (underside) of the penis. A dorsal opening describes epispadias. 595. A gravida III, para II is admitted to the labor unit. Vaginal exam reveals that the client's cervix is 8cm dilated, with complete effacement. Potential for injury related to precipitate delivery Rationale: Per Myles, a multipara (gravida III para II) at 8cm with complete effacement is in advanced active/transition labor and may deliver rapidly; the priority is preventing injury from precipitate delivery. Pain and elimination are lower priority than safety. 596. The client with varicella will most likely have an order for which category of medication? A. Antibiotics B. Antipyretics C. Antivirals D. Antivirals Rationale: Per Kenya IMNCI/clinical guidelines, varicella (chickenpox) is a viral infection; antivirals such as acyclovir are indicated in severe or high-risk cases. Ampicillin Rationale: Per Kenya EML/cardiac pharmacology, nitroglycerin, propranolol and verapamil are all appropriate for anginal chest pain; ampicillin is an antibiotic with no role in chest pain and should be questioned. 598. Which of the following instructions should be included in the teaching for the client with rheumatoid arthritis? A. Avoid exercise because it fatigues the joints. B. Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth, NSAIDs/anti-inflammatory drugs for rheumatoid arthritis should be taken with meals to reduce gastric irritation. Exercise (ROM) is encouraged, not avoided, so the other options are incorrect. 599. A client with acute pancreatitis is experiencing severe abdominal pain. During the assessment of a laboring client, the nurse notes that the FHT are loudest in the upper-right quadrant. The infant is most likely in which position? A. Right breech presentation B. Vertex presentations transmit FHTs in the lower quadrants. 601. The primary physiological alteration in the development of asthma is: A. Bronchiolar inflammation and dyspnea B. Spasm of bronchial smooth muscle Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth respiratory pathophysiology, the primary reversible physiological alteration in asthma is bronchospasm (spasm of bronchial smooth muscle), accompanied by inflammation and mucus. Bronchospasm is the hallmark driving airway narrowing. 602. To maintain Bryant's traction, the nurse must make certain that the child's: A. Buttocks must clear the mattress. 603. The client has an order for a trough to be drawn on the client receiving Vancomycin. The nurse is providing postpartum teaching for a mother planning to breastfeed her infant. Which of the client's statements indicates the need for additional teaching? A. "I'm wearing a support bra." Support bra, expressing milk, and letting water run over breasts are correct. 606. Damage to the VII cranial nerve results in: A. Facial pain B. Absence of ability to smell C. Absence of eye movement D. Tinnitus Answer: A. Facial pain Rationale: Per neuroanatomy (Brunner & Suddarth), the VII (facial) nerve controls facial muscle movement and taste; its damage causes facial weakness/paralysis and altered sensation. Smell is CN I, eye movement CN III/IV/VI, so facial involvement is the best fit among the options. ⚠ More than one defensible answer 607. A client is receiving Pyridium (phenazopyridine hydrochloride) for a urinary tract infection. The client should be taught that the medication may: A. Cause diarrhea B. Change the color of her urine C. Cause mental confusion D. Cause changes in taste Answer: B. Change the color of her urine Rationale: Per Kenya EML/pharmacology, phenazopyridine (Pyridium) is a urinary analgesic that characteristically turns urine reddish-orange; clients must be forewarned to avoid alarm and staining. It does not typically cause diarrhea or confusion. 608. Which of the following tests should be performed before beginning a prescription of Accutane? A. Check the calcium level B. Perform a pregnancy test Rationale: Per pharmacology (Kenya EML/BNF), isotretinoin (Accutane) is highly teratogenic, so a negative pregnancy test is mandatory before starting therapy in women of childbearing potential. Nausea Rationale: Per pharmacology (Brunner & Suddarth), amphotericin B commonly causes infusion reactions such as fever, chills, nausea and, importantly, nephrotoxicity; among the listed options nausea is the recognized adverse/toxic effect. Visual changes are not characteristic. ⚠ More than one defensible answer 612. The nurse should visit which of the following clients first? A. The client with diabetes with a blood glucose of 95mg/dL B. The client with hypertension being maintained on Lisinopril C. The client with chest pain and a history of angina D. The client with Raynaud's disease Answer: C. The client with chest pain and a history of angina Rationale: Per triage/prioritization (ABC, Brunner & Suddarth), the client with active chest pain and angina history is at risk of an evolving myocardial infarction and must be seen first. The others are stable with controlled findings. 613. A client with cystic fibrosis is taking pancreatic enzymes. The nurse should administer this medication: A. Once per day in the morning B. Three times per day with meals C. Once per day at bedtime D. Four times per day Answer: B. Three times per day with meals Rationale: Pancreatic enzyme replacements (pancrelipase) must be given with each meal and snack so the enzymes are present to digest fat, protein, and carbohydrate as food enters the gut (Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing). Giving them once daily would leave most meals without enzyme support. 614. Cataracts result in opacity of the crystalline lens. Which of the following best explains the functions of the lens? A. The lens controls stimulation of the retina. B. The lens orchestrates eye movement. C. The lens focuses light rays on the retina. D. The lens magnifies small objects. Answer: C. The lens focuses light rays on the retina. Rationale: The crystalline lens refracts (focuses) incoming light rays onto the retina; cataract opacity blurs this focus (Anatomy & Physiology; Brunner & Suddarth's). Pupil/iris controls light intake and extraocular muscles control movement, not the lens. 615. A client who has glaucoma is to have miotic eye drops instilled in both eyes. The nurse knows that the purpose of the medication is to: A. Anesthetize the cornea B. Dilate the pupils C. Constrict the pupils D. Paralyze the muscles of accommodation Answer: C. Constrict the pupils Rationale: Miotics (e.g., pilocarpine) constrict the pupil, which widens the trabecular outflow and lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma (Brunner & Suddarth's; Kenya EML ophthalmic drugs). 'Miosis' means pupillary constriction, the opposite of mydriasis/dilation. 616. A client with a severe corneal ulcer has an order for Gentamicin gtt. q 4 hours and Neomycin 1 gtt q 4 hours. Which of the following schedules should be used when administering the drops? A. Allow 5 minutes between the two medications. B. The medications may be used together. C. The medications should be separated by a cycloplegic drug. D. The medications should not be used in the same client. Answer: A. Allow 5 minutes between the two medications. Rationale: When two different eye drops are ordered, a waiting interval (about 5 minutes) is required so the first drop is not washed out before absorption (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing). They should not be instilled simultaneously. 617. The client with color blindness will most likely have problems distinguishing which of the following colors? A. Orange B. Violet C. Red D. White Answer: C. Red Rationale: The most common inherited color blindness is red-green deficiency, so red is the color most likely confused (Anatomy & Physiology of vision). Violet and orange are less commonly affected and white is not a hue. 618. The client with a pacemaker should be taught to: A. Report ankle edema B. Check his blood pressure daily C. Refrain from using a microwave oven D. Monitor his pulse rate Answer: D. Monitor his pulse rate Rationale: Pacemaker clients are taught to check their pulse daily and report a rate below the set threshold, which signals pacemaker malfunction (Brunner & Suddarth's). Modern microwaves are safe, so refraining from them is unnecessary. 619. The client with enuresis is being taught regarding bladder retraining. The nurse should advise the client to refrain from drinking after: A. 1900 B. 1200 C. 1000 D. 0700 Answer: A. 1900 Rationale: In bladder retraining for enuresis, fluids are restricted in the evening (after about 1900 hrs / 7 pm) to reduce night-time bladder filling, while daytime intake stays adequate (Kozier & Erb's Fundamentals of Nursing). Stopping fluids at midday would cause dehydration. 620. Which of the following diet instructions should be given to the client with recurring urinary tract infections? A. Increase intake of meats. B. Rationale: Cranberry juice acidifies urine and inhibits bacterial adherence to the bladder wall, helping prevent recurrent UTIs (Brunner & Suddarth's). Citrus need not be avoided, and hydrogen peroxide pericare is inappropriate. 621. The physician has prescribed NPH insulin for a client with diabetes mellitus. Which statement indicates that the client knows when the peak action of the insulin occurs? A. "I will make sure I eat breakfast within 2 hours of taking my insulin." B. "I will need to carry candy or some form of sugar with me all the time." C. "I will eat a snack around three o'clock each afternoon." D. "I can save my dessert from supper for a bedtime snack." Answer: C. "I will eat a snack around three o'clock each afternoon." Rationale: NPH (intermediate-acting) insulin peaks roughly 6-12 hours after a morning dose, so a mid-afternoon snack covers the peak and prevents hypoglycemia (Brunner & Suddarth's; Kenya EML). Eating breakfast within 2 hours describes rapid/short-acting insulin. 622. A client with pneumocystis carinii pneumonia is receiving trimetrexate. The rationale for administering leucovorin calcium to a client receiving Methotrexate is to: A. Treat anemia. B. Create a synergistic effect. C. Increase the number of white blood cells. D. Reverse drug toxicity. Answer: D. Reverse drug toxicity. Rationale: Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue counteracts the folate-antagonist toxicity of methotrexate/trimetrexate, protecting normal cells (Brunner & Suddarth's; Kenya EML). It is a rescue agent, not a synergistic or hematinic agent. 623. A client tells the nurse that she is allergic to eggs, dogs, rabbits, and chicken feathers. Which order should the nurse question? A. Rubella vaccine Rationale: MMR/rubella vaccine is cultured in chick embryo cells, so a documented severe egg allergy warrants questioning the order (Brunner & Suddarth's; KEPI cautions). TB skin test, ELISA, and chest x-ray carry no egg-protein risk. 624. The physician has prescribed ranitidine (Zantac) for a client with erosive gastritis. In a single dose at bedtime D. 60 minutes after meals Answer: A. 30 minutes before meals Rationale: H2 antagonists such as ranitidine are best given before meals so the drug blocks the acid secretion stimulated by eating (Brunner & Suddarth's; Kenya EML). Single bedtime dosing does not cover mealtime acid surges as well. 625. A temporary colostomy is performed on the client with colon cancer. The nurse is aware that the proximal end of a double barrel colostomy: A. Is the opening on the client's left side B. Is the opening on the distal end on the client's left side C. Is the opening on the client's right side Rationale: In a double-barrel colostomy the proximal (functioning) stoma is on the client's right, following the direction of bowel flow from the ascending/transverse colon, while the distal non-functioning stoma is on the left (Brunner & Suddarth's). 626. While assessing the postpartal client, the nurse notes that the fundus is displaced to the right. Based on this finding, the nurse should: A. Ask the client to void B. Ask the client to void Rationale: A fundus displaced to the right (and often above the umbilicus) indicates a full bladder; having the client void allows the uterus to recenter and contract, preventing atony (Myles Textbook for Midwives; Kenya MNH guidelines). Oxytocin is not first-line for a bladder-related displacement. 627. The physician has ordered an MRI for a client with an orthopedic ailment. An MRI should not be done if the client has: A. The need for oxygen therapy B. A history of claustrophobia C. A permanent pacemaker D. Sensory deafness Answer: C. A permanent pacemaker Rationale: MRI is contraindicated with most permanent pacemakers because the strong magnetic field can disrupt or damage the device (Brunner & Suddarth's). Claustrophobia and deafness can be accommodated and are not absolute contraindications. 628. A 6-month-old client is placed on strict bed rest following a hernia repair. Colorful crib mobile Rationale: A colorful crib mobile suits a 6-month-old's developmental level (visual tracking) and is appropriate for strict bed rest (Basic Paediatric Protocols; growth & development principles). Electronic games and jigsaw puzzles are for older children. 629. The nurse is preparing to discharge a client with a long history of polio. The nurse should tell the client that: A. Taking a hot bath will decrease stiffness and spasticity. B. A schedule of strenuous exercise will improve muscle strength. C. Rest periods should be scheduled throughout the day. D. Visual disturbances can be corrected with prescription glasses. Answer: C. Rest periods should be scheduled throughout the day. Rationale: Clients with polio/post-polio syndrome fatigue easily, so scheduled rest periods conserve energy and protect weakened muscles (Brunner & Suddarth's). Strenuous exercise can worsen muscle weakness and is contraindicated. 630. A client on the postpartum unit has a proctoepisiotomy. The nurse should anticipate administering which medication? A. Rationale: TPN is a hypertonic high-dextrose solution that commonly causes hyperglycemia, requiring sliding-scale insulin coverage (Brunner & Suddarth's). The primary reason for rapid continuous rewarming of the area affected by frostbite is to: A. Lessen the amount of cellular damage B. Prevent the formation of blisters C. Promote movement D. Prevent pain and discomfort Answer: A. A client recently started on hemodialysis wants to know how the dialysis will take the place of his kidneys. The nurse's response is based on the knowledge that hemodialysis works by: A. Passing water through a dialyzing membrane B. Eliminating plasma proteins from the blood C. Lowering the pH by removing nonvolatile acids D. Filtering waste through a dialyzing membrane Answer: D. Filtering waste through a dialyzing membrane Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth's, hemodialysis removes nitrogenous waste and excess solutes by diffusion across a semipermeable dialyzing membrane; it does not remove plasma proteins and its purpose is waste filtration, not simply passing water. 647. During a home visit, a client with AIDS tells the nurse that he has been exposed to measles. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate? A. Administer an antibiotic B. A client who is admitted with an above-the-knee amputation tells the nurse that his foot hurts and itches. Which response by the nurse indicates understanding of phantom limb pain? A. "The pain is due to peripheral nervous system interruptions. I will get you some pain medication." Rationale: Per Brunner & Suddarth's, phantom limb pain is a real physiologic phenomenon arising from severed peripheral nerve pathways and CNS reorganization, not psychological; it should be acknowledged and treated with analgesia. 649. A client with cancer of the pancreas has undergone a Whipple procedure. The nurse is aware that during the Whipple procedure, the doctor will remove the: A. Head of the pancreas B. The nurse is assisting the physician with removal of a central venous catheter. To facilitate removal, the nurse should instruct the client to: A. Source: NCK Paper 1 & 2 Combined Practice Sets (Type 1-4) 662. The physical manifestations of fetal alcohol syndrome include: A. cleft lip and palette. B. hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and microphthalmia. Effective supplementation of folate for prevention of neural tube defect is A. started at least 1 mo before conception, and continued through the first 2-3 mo of pregnancy B. started at least 3 mo before conception, to be stopped after positive pregnancy C. started after positive pregnancy test and continued through the first 2-3 mo of pregnancy. Expansion of the intravascular volume and increased intravascular pressure are the main causes of edema in A. lymphatic obstruction B. heart failure C. protein-losing enteropathy D. nephrotic syndrome Answer: B. heart failure Rationale: In heart failure, increased intravascular (venous/hydrostatic) volume and pressure drive fluid into interstitium causing oedema; per Brunner & Suddarth's Medical-Surgical Nursing. Lymphatic obstruction, protein-losing enteropathy and nephrotic syndrome cause oedema mainly via reduced oncotic pressure or lymphatic blockage, not raised intravascular volume/pressure. 668. Increased production of CO2 occurs in all the following EXCEPT A. fever B. emesis C. excess caloric intake D. high levels of physical activity Answer: B. emesis Rationale: Fever, excess caloric intake and high physical activity all raise metabolic rate and CO2 production; per Brunner & Suddarth acid-base physiology. Emesis (vomiting) does not increase CO2 production (it causes loss of gastric acid), so it is the EXCEPT answer. 669. Malignant hyperthermia is an acute hypermetabolic syndrome that is triggered by inhalational anesthetic agents and succinylcholine. Of the following, the MOST recognized clue to the risk of malignant hyperthermia is A. rigid clenching of the masseter muscles B. hypercarbia C. ventricular fibrillation D. rapid onset of fever Answer: A. rigid clenching of the masseter muscles Rationale: Masseter muscle rigidity (trismus) after succinylcholine is the earliest and most recognized clinical clue to malignant hyperthermia; per Brunner & Suddarth peri-operative/anesthesia nursing. Hypercarbia, arrhythmias and fever occur but appear later and are less specific as the initiating clue. 670. Cyanosis (unresponsive to oxygen) is a sign of poisoning with A. atropine B. amiodarone C. carbon monoxide D. vancomycin Answer: C. carbon monoxide Rationale: Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen indicates that haemoglobin cannot carry/release oxygen, characteristic of carbon monoxide poisoning (and methaemoglobinaemia); per Brunner & Suddarth/toxicology. Atropine, amiodarone and vancomycin do not classically cause oxygen-refractory cyanosis. 671. The MOST common reason for a sick child visit is A. vomiting B. altered mental status C. respiratory distress D. fever Answer: D. fever Rationale: Fever is the single most common presenting complaint for sick child visits; per Kenya IMNCI and Basic Paediatric Protocols. Vomiting, altered mental status and respiratory distress are common but less frequent than fever as the chief complaint. 672. Major cause of neonatal mortality in full-term newborn is A. respiratory distress syndrome B. necrotizing enterocolitis C. bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) D. congenital anomalies Answer: D. congenital anomalies Rationale: In full-term newborns, congenital anomalies are the leading cause of neonatal mortality; per Kenya newborn care/Basic Paediatric Protocols. RDS, NEC and BPD predominate in preterm rather than term infants. 673. Common respiratory tract manifestations of neonatal bacterial infections is A. ethmoiditis B. empyema C. otitis media D. mastoiditis Answer: C. otitis media Rationale: Otitis media is a common upper respiratory tract manifestation of neonatal bacterial infection; per Basic Paediatric Protocols/neonatal texts. Ethmoiditis, empyema and mastoiditis are uncommon in neonates as presenting infections. ⚠ More than one defensible answer 674. Freedom of choice in one of the policies of the Family Planning Program. Which of the following illustrates this principle? A. Information dissemination about the need for family planning B. Support of research and development in family planning methods C. . Adequate information for couples regarding the different methods Rationale: Freedom of choice is exercised when couples are given adequate information on all available methods so they can choose freely; per Kenya National Family Planning Guidelines. General information dissemination (A), research support (B) and encouraging joint responsibility (D) do not directly embody informed free choice among methods. 675. Scotch tape swab is done to check for which intestinal parasite? A. Ascaris B. . Pinworm C. . Hookworm D. Schistosoma Answer: B. . Which of the following opportunistic infections is characterized by tonsilllopharyngitis? A. Respiratory candidiasis B. . Infectious mononucleosis C. Cytomegalovirus disease D. Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia Answer: B. . Infectious mononucleosis Rationale: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) classically presents with tonsillopharyngitis (exudative pharyngitis), fever and lymphadenopathy; per Brunner & Suddarth, EBV is a common opportunistic reactivation in immunosuppressed/AIDS patients. Antiretroviral agents, such as AZT are used in the management of AIDS. Which of the following is not an action expected of these drugs? A. They prolong the life of the client with AIDS B. . They reduce the risk of opportunistic infections C. . They shorten the period of communicability of the disease D. They are able to bring about a cure of the disease condition Your Answer : Answer: D. They are able to bring about a cure of the disease condition Your Answer : Rationale: Per Kenya National ARV Guidelines, ART suppresses viral replication, prolongs life, reduces opportunistic infections and lowers communicability, but does NOT cure HIV. The question asks which is NOT an expected action, so the correct answer is that ARVs cure the disease. 678. A 1 1/2 year old child was classified as having 3rd degree of protein energy malnutrition, kwashjorkor. Which of the following signs will be most apparent in this child? A. voracious appetite B. wasting C. apathy D. edema Answer: D. edema Rationale: Per Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols and IMNCI, kwashiorkor (protein malnutrition) is characterised chiefly by bilateral pitting oedema, along with apathy and hair/skin changes; oedema is the defining/most apparent sign distinguishing it from marasmus (wasting). Wasting is the hallmark of marasmus, not kwashiorkor. 679. abnrmally low set ears could be indicative of A. otogenous tetanus B. congenital heart defect C. tracheoesophageal fistula D. renal anomalies Answer: D. renal anomalies Rationale: Per paediatric/neonatal assessment (Basic Paediatric Protocols; standard paediatric texts), low-set ears are a well-recognised marker associated with congenital renal anomalies (and chromosomal syndromes) because the ears and kidneys develop concurrently. This is the classic newborn examination association. 680. in type three trachea-esophageal fistula A. upper segment of esophagus open into trachea B. lower segment of esophagus open into trachea C. normal trachea and esophagus are connected by a fistula D. proximal and distal segments of esophagus are blind Answer: C. normal trachea and esophagus are connected by a fistula Rationale: Per paediatric surgery classification (Gross type C, the most common tracheo-esophageal fistula), Type III/C is a proximal esophageal atresia with a distal esophageal segment communicating with the trachea via a fistula — i.e. trachea and esophagus connected by a fistula. This is the commonest variant taught in paediatric nursing. ⚠ More than one defensible answer 681. A mother brought her daughter, 4 years old, to the RHU because of cough and colds. Inability to drink is a listed IMNCI danger sign; high fever and cough duration are not general danger signs. 682. Management of a child with measles includes the administration of which of the following? A. Gentian violet on mouth lesions B. Antibiotic to prevent pneumonia C. A mother brought her 10 month old infant for consultation because of fever which started 4 days prior to consultation. To determine malaria risk, what will you do? A. Do a tourniquet test B. They are not found on the nasal mucosa or skin. 685. In a mother’s class, you discuss proper breastfeeding technique. Which of these is a sign that the baby has “lactated on” the breast property? A. This pairing is the recognised complication set. 688. Maternal factors that may interfere with breast feeding include:- A. Infections, prematurity, birth injuries B. Molly, with suspected rheumatic fever, is admitted to the pediatric unit. When obtaining the child’s history, the nurse considers which information to be most important? A. By the age of 7 months the infant is able to do all the following EXCEPT A. transfer object from hand to hand B. bounces actively C. cruises D. grasp uses radial palm Answer: C. cruises Rationale: Per paediatric growth and development, a 7-month-old can transfer objects hand to hand, bounce actively, and use a radial-palmar grasp, but cruising (walking while holding furniture) is not achieved until about 9-12 months, making it the EXCEPTION. 698. The neurodevelopmental function (cognition) is dependent mainly on the development of the following functions EXCEPT A. sensory and motor B. language C. visual–spatial D. cerebeller Answer: D. cerebeller Rationale: Neurodevelopmental cognition depends on sensory-motor, language and visual-spatial streams (Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics). Emergency treatment in severe malnutrition includes all the following EXCEPT A. infections B. severe anemia C. dehydration and shock D. hypoglycemia Answer: B. severe anemia Rationale: Immediate emergency threats in severe acute malnutrition are hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration/shock and infection (WHO 10 steps; Kenya Basic Paediatric Protocols). Thus pinkish skin is the exception. 728. A mother would like to know the reason why there is asthma in her child. How would you explain it? A. Cervical cancer Rationale: Per Kenya cervical cancer screening/national guidelines, human papillomavirus (HPV, esp. types 16/18) is the principal cause of cervical cancer. 104. During the initial interview, the client reports that she has a lesion on the perineum. Further investigation reveals a small blister on the vulva that is painful to touch. The nurse is aware that the most likely source of the lesion is: A. Syphilis B. Herpes C. Gonorrhea D. Condylomata . Answer: B. Fluorescent treponemal antibody (FTA) Rationale: Per STI diagnostic guidelines, FTA-ABS is a specific treponemal antibody test confirming Treponema pallidum; VDRL and RPR are non-specific screening (non-treponemal) tests and Thayer-Martin is for gonorrhoea. 106. The client is admitted to the chemical dependence unit with an order for continuous observation. The nurse is aware that the doctor has ordered continuous observation because: A. Rationale: Per mental health nursing (Kozier/psychiatric texts), hallucinogens cause altered perception and distorted reality that can lead to unpredictable, unsafe behavior, warranting continuous observation. They do not cause severe respiratory depression or rapid physical dependence. 107. A client with a history of abusing barbiturates abruptly stops taking the medication. Euphoria and diarrhea are not typical barbiturate withdrawal features. ⚠ More than one defensible answer 108. A client with mania is unable to finish her dinner. Serve high-calorie foods she can carry with her Rationale: Per psychiatric nursing (Kozier), a client in mania is too hyperactive to sit and eat, so providing high-calorie finger foods she can carry while moving maintains nutrition. Sitting for small portions or waiting for favorite foods is impractical during mania. 109. Which action by the nurse indicates understanding of herpes zoster? A. Rationale: Per infection prevention (Kenya IPC guidelines), herpes zoster lesion fluid is infectious (contact/airborne precautions), so wearing gloves during care prevents transmission. It is viral, so antibiotics are not indicated. 110. A client is brought to the emergency room by the police. He is combative and yells, "I have to get out of here. They are trying to kill me." It is a thought-content disturbance, not an auditory hallucination or a grandiose delusion. 111. The nurse is preparing to suction the client with a tracheotomy. A client hospitalized with MRSA (methicillin-resistant staph aureus) is placed on contact precautions. Which statement is true regarding precautions for infections spread by contact? A. Rationale: Per Kenya IPC guidelines, contact precautions (e.g., MRSA) rely on hand hygiene, gloves and gowns to prevent direct/indirect contact spread; negative-pressure rooms and masks are airborne precautions, not contact. 113.
